How do we understand a variable?
Before any model, any test, any result — you need to know what your data actually looks like.

title: EDA: Understanding Your Data
text:
What is exploratory data analysis?

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the process of describing your variables — the values they take, how often they take them, and whether anything is unusual.
This is the crucial step to take before you do anything else with the data.

Békés & Kézdi frame it as three questions to ask before any model:

How should you start the analysis itself?
How do you describe the data and present its key features?
How do you explore the data and check whether it’s clean enough for further analysis?


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy, Ch. 3

title: EDA: Understanding Your Data
text:
Why bother with EDA?
Five reasons:

To check data cleaning — EDA is part of an iterative cleaning process
To guide subsequent analysis — what you see shapes what you do next
To give context for interpreting later results
To ask additional questions — EDA can refine the research question itself
It can offer simple, but possibly important, answers on its own


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3

Frequency, probability, distribution

Absolute frequency — the count of observations with a particular value
Relative frequency — that count expressed as a proportion, or percentage, of all observations
Probability generalises relative frequency: a measure of the likelihood of an event, always between 0 and 1 — and, unlike relative frequency, it can describe an event without needing a dataset at all
The distribution of a variable tells you the frequency of each value it takes in the data, independent of what the other variables show


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3

title: EDA: Understanding Your Data
text:
What is a summary statistic?
For any variable, a statistic is a meaningful number you can compute from the data. Summary statistics describe the most important features of a distribution — its centre, its spread, its shape.

Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3

title: EDA: Understanding Your Data
text:
The mean and expected value
It is standard to refer to our variable as \(x\). The mean (or average) of \(x\) is calculated as:
\[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}\] If we have \(a\) and \(b\) that are fixed whilst \(x\) varies we get two useful properties: \(\overline{x+a} = \bar{x} + a\) and \(\overline{x \cdot b} = \bar{x} \cdot b\).

The expected value, \(E[x]\), is the value you’d expect for a randomly chosen observation.

For a quantitative variable, \(E[x]\) is the mean
For a binary variable coded 0/1 — like caffeine — \(E[x]\) is the probability, or relative frequency, of the category coded 1



Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3

title: EDA: Understanding Your Data
text:
Median, quantiles, mode

Median — the middle value when sorted; half the observations lie below, half above
Quantiles / percentiles divide the data into proportions. Quartiles divide it into fourths — the median is the 2nd quartile, the 50th percentile
Mode — the most frequent value; some distributions have more than one


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3

title: EDA: Understanding Your Data
EDA: Understanding Your Data
text:
Variance and standard deviation
\[Var[x] = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1} \qquad SD[x] = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}}\]

Variance is the average squared deviation from the mean — harder to interpret directly, but easy to work with algebraically because it is itself a mean
Standard deviation is the square root of variance — back in the original units, and roughly the typical distance between a randomly chosen observation and the mean







Note


This divides by n − 1, not n — the standard formula, and what Python uses. Békés & Kézdi’s own textbook divides by n instead; the difference is small in practice, and we’ll come back to exactly why in Week 2.




Two distributions can share a mean but differ in spread: the higher the SD, the more dispersed the data. In finance, SD is literally how volatility is measured — a higher SD means a price that jumps around more.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3

title: EDA: Understanding Your Data
EDA: Understanding Your Data
text:
Standardised values and skewness
Standardising expresses a value in units of standard deviation:
\[x_{\text{standardised}} = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{SD[x]}\]
A standardised value of 1 means “one SD above the mean”; −1 means “one SD below.”

A distribution is skewed if it isn’t symmetric. A simple measure:
\[\text{Skewness} = \frac{\bar{x} - \text{median}(x)}{SD[x]}\]
When the right tail is long, the mean sits above the median and skewness is positive — exactly why our reaction-time data is right-skewed.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 3

text:
So — was a single test score enough?


Go back to HR’s onboarding test: one trial, one number, one ranking.
Every student here just produced 10 trials — and for most, the spread between fastest and slowest trial was far bigger than the difference between students.


A single measurement doesn’t tell you someone’s typical response time. It tells you where one random draw from their distribution happened to land.
HR’s test is measuring noise as if it were signal.

section: Can we claim a difference is real?
text:
Can we claim a difference is real?


We can see differences in the charts.
But is the class the population we care about?

If yes — we have all the data. No inference needed. The difference is the difference.
If no — we are treating the class as a sample from a larger group (all students? all adults?).



This is the inference question.
Any sample will show differences between groups — by chance alone.
How do we decide which differences to take seriously?
That requires thinking about sampling, variability, and probability.
That’s Week 2.

External validity
Suppose we do establish that the gap in our data is real, not chance. What exactly are we then entitled to say?

Only that it’s real for this class, on this day, using this task — not, without more work, anything about phone and laptop users in general.


That gap between what our data shows and what we’d like to claim is called external validity: whether the pattern in our data is the same as the general pattern we actually care about.


Question: what do you think external validity means for our own reaction-time gap, specifically?

title: Inference: When is a Difference Real?
text:
Three threats to external validity
Assessing whether our data represents the same general pattern we actually care about.

Time — we have data from the past (or this one session); we care about the future
Space — our data is one class, in one room, on one day; would the pattern hold elsewhere?
Sub-groups — our data is this cohort; would it hold for a different group of people?


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy, Ch. 5

One sample among many
Our Week 1 data is one dataset — one of many that could have been collected. If we ran the exercise again tomorrow, we’d get different numbers, purely by chance.

Many possible datasets = repeated samples from the same underlying data generating process
A statistic computed from data (like the mean) therefore has its own distribution — its value differs from sample to sample.

Today’s mean will differ from tomorrows.

That distribution is called the statistic’s sampling distribution, and it is a different object from the distribution of the variable itself

But we don’t actually know the DGP
Everything so far assumed a known population — Normal(μ, σ) — so we could watch 1,000 simulated samples land around the true value.

In reality, we have one dataset: the reaction-time data collected last week. No known μ, no known σ, no ability to simulate 1,000 more classes.
Two ways forward: a formula, or a computational trick called the bootstrap.

The standard error formula
\[SE(\bar{x}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \, SD[x]\]

Larger when the data is more spread out (SD[x] larger)
Smaller when the sample is bigger (n larger)


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 5

The bootstrap idea

Take the original dataset and draw repeated samples from it, with replacement
Each draw can be picked more than once; some observations won’t be picked at all
Compute the statistic (e.g. the mean) on each resample
The spread of those resampled statistics approximates the sampling distribution — without ever needing to know the true DGP

text:
What is a confidence interval?
A confidence interval (CI) is a range where we expect the true value — in the population, or general pattern, that our data represents — to fall, with a probability we choose. Analysts typically pick 95%, sometimes 90% or 99%.

From the perspective of a single sample: there is a 95% chance that the true value lies within this interval — and a 5% chance it doesn’t. We don’t know - we can’t know - which case we’re in.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 5

title: Inference: When is a Difference Real?
text:
Building the interval
A CI is a symmetric range around the estimated value, built from the SE:
\[CI = \text{statistic} \; \pm \; (\text{critical value} \times SE)\]



Confidence level
Critical value




90%
1.6 × SE


95%
2 × SE


99%
2.6 × SE




Wider interval → more confident it contains the truth, but less precise about where. There’s no free lunch: more confidence costs precision.

Task — does the bootstrap agree with the formula?


n starts at our real class sample size, but with only 10 resamples — read off the bootstrap SE.

Now drag n down to a small value. What happens to the spread of the histogram? Which property of the sampling distribution does that demonstrate?



Under the conditions we need — large enough sample, independent observations — the bootstrap and the formula converge on the same answer. The formula is faster; the bootstrap works even when no formula exists.
Dragging n down widens the bootstrap histogram — the same root-n convergence we saw earlier (SE shrinks as n grows), now showing up in a resampled statistic instead of a formula.

Quick recap

We want to generalise from our data — statistical inference
Two ways to estimate the uncertainty in a statistic: a formula (\(SE = SD/\sqrt{n}\)) or the bootstrap (resample with replacement, look at the spread)
Under the conditions the formula needs, the two agree — but the bootstrap keeps working even when no formula exists
A 95% CI is the estimate ± 2 × SE — a range we expect to contain the true value, and 95% of intervals built this way actually do
Using the CI, we can now make a statement about the population, or general pattern, that our data represents

text: Testing a hypothesis

title: Inference: When is a Difference Real?
text:
Fisher’s tea test

A woman claims she can tell, by taste, whether the milk or the tea was poured into the cup first.
Ronald Fisher didn’t just take her word for it — and he didn’t dismiss her either. He designed a test: several cups, milk-first and tea-first in random order, unknown to her. She has to identify all of them correctly.


If she’s just guessing, we can calculate exactly how likely she is to get them all right by chance. If she does far better than chance predicts, that’s evidence for her claim.
This is the entire logic of hypothesis testing, built from one experiment in 1920s Cambridge.

title: Inference: When is a Difference Real?
text:
The null is protected
Testing a hypothesis means asking: is there enough evidence in the data to reject a default, protected assumption?


Criminal court

Assume innocence
Only convict if evidence is strong
“Not guilty” ≠ proven innocent — just not enough evidence



Hypothesis testing

\(H_0\) (null): protected, assumed true until shown otherwise
\(H_A\) (alternative): what we suspect instead
Failing to reject \(H_0\) ≠ proving it true — just not enough evidence




Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 6

No true difference in reaction time by device, versus: there is one.

title: Inference: When is a Difference Real?
text:
The t-statistic
The test statistic measures how far our estimate is from what \(H_0\) predicts, in units of standard error.
\[t = \frac{\hat{s}}{SE(\hat{s})}\]
For a difference between two averages, \(\bar{x}_A\) and \(\bar{x}_B\):
\[t = \frac{\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B}{SE(\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B)} \qquad SE(\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B) = \sqrt{\frac{SD_A^2}{n_A} + \frac{SD_B^2}{n_B}}\]

Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 6

What if we had 15,000 students, not 15?

With a huge sample, almost any difference becomes statistically significant — the CI narrows to nearly nothing, and even a 1ms gap could reject \(H_0\).


Statistical significance ≠ practical significance. At scale, the question shifts from “is there a difference?” to “is the difference big enough to matter?” — external validity remains just as important as it was at n=15.

Recap — how do we know a difference is real?

Sampling distributions: any statistic computed from a sample has its own distribution across repeated samples from the same DGP — that’s why a single estimate is never the whole story
Standard error: a formula (\(SE = SD/\sqrt{n}\)) or the bootstrap — two ways to estimate how much a statistic would vary from sample to sample
Confidence intervals: statistic ± critical value × SE — a range built so that, over many samples, it contains the true value a chosen % of the time
Hypothesis testing: state \(H_0\), compute a t-statistic, compare it to a critical value (±1.96 for 5%) or read off the p-value directly
Two ways to be wrong: false positives (Type I) and false negatives (Type II) — the test is designed to protect against false positives
Statistical ≠ practical significance: with a big enough sample almost anything is “significant” — effect size and external validity still matter

title: Testing Pitfalls
text:
Testing pitfalls
The workshop built the t-test. This session covers how it’s misused — and how to pick your thresholds properly.

title: Testing Pitfalls
text:
One-sided vs. two-sided tests
So far we’ve tested \(H_0: s_{true} = 0\) against \(H_A: s_{true} \neq 0\) — a two-sided test, since we don’t care about the direction of the difference.

Example: does device affect reaction time? We had no prior reason to expect phones faster than laptops, or vice versa — either direction would be a meaningful finding, so both tails count as evidence against \(H_0\).
Reject \(H_0\) if \(|t| > c\) — the t-statistic is extreme in either direction. For a 5% test, \(c \approx 1.96\): this is the same \(\pm 2\) rule from the workshop, with the 5% split across both tails (2.5% each).


A one-sided test focuses on one direction only:
\[H_0: s_{true} \leq 0 \quad \text{vs.} \quad H_A: s_{true} > 0\]
Example: does caffeine reduce reaction time? Caffeine is a stimulant — we have a specific directional prediction going in, so only a large effect in that one predicted direction counts as evidence against \(H_0\).
Reject \(H_0\) if \(t > c\) — extreme in the predicted direction only. For a 5% test, \(c \approx 1.645\): smaller than the two-sided threshold, because all 5% sits in one tail instead of being split.


Same overall false-positive rate (5%) either way — but the one-sided test is more powerful for an effect in the predicted direction (a smaller \(t\) clears the lower bar), at the cost of zero power to detect an effect in the other direction, however large.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 6

title: Testing Pitfalls
section: What p-value threshold should you pick?
text:
What p-value threshold should you pick?
There’s no universal answer — it’s a trade-off, and it depends on what’s at stake.







Scenario
Suggested threshold




“Guilty beyond reasonable doubt” — a costly, hard-to-reverse decision
Conservative: 1% or lower


“Proof of concept” — deciding whether to investigate further
Looser: 10–15% is often fine




A result significant at 10–15% is still informative — it’s much more likely to be real than not. It just means: worth another look, more data, more experimentation, before betting the business on it.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 6

title: Testing Pitfalls
text:
Size and power
Size of the test — under \(H_0\): the probability of a false positive. We fix this in advance (usually 5% or 1%) — the level of significance.
Power of the test — under \(H_A\): the probability of avoiding a false negative.

Power is higher when:

the sample is larger
the dispersion (SD) is smaller
the true effect is further from the null

title: Testing Pitfalls
Testing Pitfalls
text:
Multiple testing: the motivation
A medical dataset: 400 patients, a heart-disease indicator, and 100 lifestyle features — diet, exercise, income, sleep, dozens more.

Test each feature against heart disease, one by one, at 5% significance. You find six with a “significant” link.
Is that a discovery?

title: Testing Pitfalls
text:
Simply by chance
If all 100 null hypotheses were actually true — no real links exist anywhere — a 5% false-positive rate means we’d still expect to reject 5 of them, purely by chance.

Picking out those five and writing them up as findings is exactly backwards: we started by assuming none of them were real.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 6

title: Testing Pitfalls
text:
The jelly bean problem

  
    
  


XKCD #882, “Significant” — Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5 — click to view full size

title: Testing Pitfalls
text:
Fixing it
Testing many hypotheses at once needs a stricter bar than testing one.

Simple fix: for a few dozen tests, use a much stricter threshold — 0.1–0.5% instead of 5%
Bonferroni correction: divide your target p-value by the number of tests. Aiming for 5% across 20 hypotheses → reject only below 0.05/20 = 0.0025
Often criticised as too strict — but a reasonable default when you don’t know better


p-hacking: running many tests (or many versions of one test) and reporting only the ones that “worked.” The jelly-bean comic, deliberately.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 6

title: Testing Pitfalls
section: Testing when the data is huge
text:
Testing when the data is huge
With millions of observations, statistical inference starts to lose relevance — confidence intervals become vanishingly narrow, and almost any difference becomes “statistically significant,” including ones too small to matter economically.

The question shifts from “is there a difference?” to “is the difference big enough to matter?” — look at the size of the effect, not just whether it clears a p-value bar.
External validity remains just as important at scale as it was with 15 observations.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 5 & 6

title: Testing Pitfalls
text:
AI: asking for a formula
Gabor & Kézdi tried asking an AI for the two-sample t-test formula. It came back mostly right — but “mostly” is the operative word.

AI tools are good at explaining concepts, deriving formulas, and calculating statistics from data you give them. Use them that way — but check the output, the same way you’d check a classmate’s working. Wrong formulas read just as fluently as right ones.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 5 & 6

When y met x
Weeks 1–2 looked at one variable at a time. Today: how do two variables move together — and when should we trust that?

title: When y Met x: Correlation and Covariance
text:
A shortcut for HR

The reaction-time test works, but it takes ten trials per person to administer. HR wants something faster: “find us a quick physical measurement that predicts reaction time, and we’ll screen candidates on that instead.”


That’s why we collected index finger length back in Week 1.
Is it a fast, reliable stand-in for the real test? Today gives us the tools to answer that properly — and the discipline not to answer it too quickly.

title: When y Met x: Correlation and Covariance
text:
The y and the x
Much of data analysis is about comparing values of a y variable across values of an x variable — uncovering patterns of association.

By convention, y is the variable we’re interested in; x is what we compare across
Goal 1 — prediction: use x to predict y, without needing to know why
Goal 2 — causal effect: learn what would happen to y if we changed x


HR’s proxy-test idea is a prediction goal, dressed up as if it were free of that distinction. Keep watching for where the two goals get blurred.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy, Ch. 4

text: Conditional probability

title: When y Met x: Correlation and Covariance
text:
Conditioning on x

Comparison → conditioning. Comparing y by values of x means we condition y on x
x is the conditioning variable; y is the outcome variable
Conditional probability: \(P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}\)
Joint probability: \(P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)\) — if A and B are independent
Independence: \(P(A \mid B) = P(A)\) and \(P(B \mid A) = P(B)\)


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4

On paper, using the table above: what is \(P(\text{Caffeine} = \text{Yes} \mid \text{Device} = \text{Phone})\)?
Does knowing someone’s device change your guess about their caffeine use? How much would you trust that conclusion, given how many observations it’s based on?


Independence is not a yes/no question you can answer from a table this small. Any real sample will show some numerical gap between the conditional and marginal probabilities, purely by chance — even when the true population relationship is independence. Telling a real pattern from sampling noise is exactly what Week 2’s tools (standard errors, hypothesis tests) are for. With this few observations, “we can’t tell yet” is the honest answer, not a verdict either way.

The conditional expectation of y for a given value of x:
\[E[y \mid x]\]

The mean of y, computed separately for each value (or group) of x
With few x values, a histogram or box plot per group works well (Week 1)
With many x values — like finger length in mm — group into bins first

text:
Covariance
In plain language: covariance asks whether x and y tend to move together — when one is above its own average, is the other usually above its average too?

\[Cov[x,y] = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{n}\]

Multiplies each observation’s deviation from the x-mean by its deviation from the y-mean, and averages
Positive when x and y tend to deviate from their means in the same direction
Can be any positive or negative number — units depend on the units of x and y



Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4

title: When y Met x: Correlation and Covariance
When y Met x: Correlation and Covariance
text:
Correlation
In plain language: correlation asks the same question as covariance — do x and y move together — but reports the answer on a fixed scale from −1 to 1, so it’s comparable no matter what units x and y are measured in.
The standardised version of the covariance — divide by the product of the standard deviations:
\[Corr[x,y] = \frac{Cov[x,y]}{SD[x] \, SD[y]} \qquad -1 \leq Corr[x,y] \leq 1\]
Rough guide: below 0.2 is weak, above 0.7 is generally strong.

title: When y Met x: Correlation and Covariance
section: Where does the variation in x come from?
text:
Where does the variation in x come from?
Comparison requires variation in the conditioning variable — and where that variation comes from matters enormously.


Experimental data

A treatment is assigned, often randomly
Differences in y are attributable to the treatment alone
e.g. randomly assign aspirin vs. placebo



Observational data

x varies because of people’s own choices, circumstances, history
Many other things may differ alongside x
e.g. people who already take aspirin routinely may do so because of prior health risk




Almost everything in business analytics is observational. Finger length is one of the few genuinely fixed, “as-if-random” variables we’re likely to find — most x’s we’ll meet from here on are not.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4

text:

Go to tylervigen.com/spurious-correlations. Find one example. In one sentence, explain why the two variables move together despite having no plausible causal link.


Correlation, on its own, never tells you which of these is true: x causes y, y causes x, both are caused by something else, or coincidence.

text: Measuring what you can’t observe directly

title: When y Met x: Correlation and Covariance
text:
Latent variables
Some concepts — attitude, ability, management quality — can’t be measured with a single variable. They’re latent: real, but only indirectly observable through several proxies at once.

Use one variable — simple, but throws away information
Average several (as z-scores) — standardise first, then average; simple and transparent
PCA — weights each variable by how well it captures the shared pattern; typically close to the simple average in practice


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4

title: When y Met x: Correlation and Covariance
text:
Use one variable
The simplest approach: pick a single observable variable and treat it as a stand-in for the thing you can’t measure directly.

Postcode as a proxy for socioeconomic background
Job tenure as a proxy for “experience”
Finger length as a proxy for manual dexterity — this module’s own opening example


It’s simple, and sometimes good enough. But a single proxy only ever captures part of the underlying concept — whatever it misses is thrown away, and if the proxy is a weak one, most of the concept goes with it.



Task — our own reaction times aren’t purely mechanical. What latent variables might actually be driving them — alertness, familiarity with the device, motivation on the day? What proxies do we already have sitting in our own data for any of these?

AI and finding patterns
GenAI is genuinely useful for a first pass over a new dataset — spotting candidate patterns quickly, the way a quick script or profiler would.

Where it’s weaker: judging whether a correlation is meaningfully weak or strong, and knowing which pattern is worth pursuing in the first place. That judgment is still yours.

title: Functional Form: Why We Log
text:
Why we log
The workshop used the log of reaction time to see a pattern more clearly. This session looks at why that works — and when it stops working.

title: Functional Form: Why We Log
text:
Why transform at all?
A “% change” needs a baseline — a “before” to measure against. Time series has one built in: this year’s GDP vs. last year’s.

Cross-sectional data doesn’t. Student A’s finger length isn’t “before” Student B’s — there’s no natural reference point to build a percentage difference from.


The natural logarithm sidesteps the problem: on a log scale, the difference between any two values approximates their percentage difference — no designated baseline required. It has a second payoff too: frequent nonlinear patterns are often far better approximated once we look at relative differences instead of raw ones.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy, Ch. 4

title: Functional Form: Why We Log
text:
What ln(x) actually buys you

\(\ln(x)\) = the natural logarithm of \(x\) — \(x\) must be a positive number: \(\ln(0)\) and \(\ln(\text{negative})\) don’t exist, so a variable with zeros (e.g. income including the unemployed) can’t be logged as-is
The claim: differences in natural logs approximate relative (percentage) differences

\[\ln(x + \Delta x) - \ln(x) \approx \frac{\Delta x}{x}\]

Numerically: \(\ln(1.01) = 0.0099 \approx 0.01\) — a 1% increase. \(\ln(1.1) = 0.095 \approx 0.1\) — close to a 10% increase, already a little off.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4

title: Functional Form: Why We Log
text:
Where it comes from
From calculus: the derivative of \(\ln(x)\) is \(\dfrac{1}{x}\).
\[\frac{d\ln(x)}{dx} = \frac{1}{x} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \ln(x+\Delta x) - \ln(x) \approx \frac{1}{x}\Delta x = \frac{\Delta x}{x}\]

That’s the whole trick: a log difference is approximately a relative difference, for small changes. The approximation is a straight line touching the curve — it only stays close nearby.

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
Simple regression
Week 3 found a weak correlation. Today: turn that into a model, and be honest about what it’s worth.

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
From correlation to formula

Week 3 found a weak correlation between finger length and reaction time. HR wants to know: can we turn that into an actual formula — a screening tool?


Naive answer: draw a line through the points, read off the equation, done.
Why it’s not that simple: which line, by what criterion? What does the slope actually mean? And a weak correlation doesn’t become a good predictor just because you fit a line through it.

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text: What is regression?

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
Regression: comparing conditional means
Regression uncovers the pattern of association between y (the outcome we care about) and x — by comparing the average value of y across different values of x.
\[E[y \mid x] = f(x) \qquad \text{shorthand: } y^E = f(x)\]

Non-parametric regression — no functional form imposed; flexible, but needs many observations per x value (this is exactly the bin-scatter from Week 3)
Parametric regression — imposes a functional form (e.g. linear); more restrictive, but interpretable with far less data


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy, Ch. 7

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
Non-parametric regression: LOWESS
Bin-scatter gives one average per bracket. LOWESS (locally weighted scatterplot smoothing, “loess”) gives a smooth curve instead — a predicted value at every x, not just at bin midpoints.

It’s a moving, weighted local average: points near x count a lot, points far from x count little
The bandwidth controls how “local” — wide = smoother, but can miss real bends; narrow = tracks the pattern closely, but looks rugged
Like bin-scatter: great for spotting shape, gives no interpretable number


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 7

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
section: Try a bandwidth on our own data

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
Two goals, kept separate

Predictive analysis — what to expect of y for a given x. Concerned with the predicted value.
Causal analysis — the effect of x on y. Concerned with a parameter — what would y be if we changed x?


Regression itself doesn’t know which goal you have. It’s a method of comparison either way — the interpretation you’re allowed to make is what changes.

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text: Linear regression

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
From y to \(y^E\)
Every individual observation’s y is really:
\[y = \alpha + \beta x + \varepsilon\]

\(\varepsilon\) is everything else affecting y — other factors, individual noise, luck. We never observe it directly.
Key assumption: \(E[\varepsilon \mid x] = 0\) — on average, the error is unrelated to x; x tells us nothing about which way \(\varepsilon\) leans.


Take the expectation of both sides:
\[E[y \mid x] = \alpha + \beta x + \underbrace{E[\varepsilon \mid x]}_{=\,0} = \alpha + \beta x\]
The error term doesn’t vanish from reality — it averages to zero by assumption. What’s left is exactly \(y^E\): our shorthand for “the part of y that x explains, once the noise is averaged away.”


Individual students will still scatter around this line by their own \(\varepsilon\) — as the finger length isn’t the only thing driving reaction time.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 7

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
Imposing a line
\[y^E = \alpha + \beta x\]

Linear regression imposes linearity in the coefficients — the simplest parametric form
Two coefficients: the intercept (\(\alpha\)) and the slope (\(\beta\))
Linearity is an assumption, or an approximation — even if the true pattern curves, a line approximates its average slope


\(\alpha\): the average value of y when x is zero —
\[E[y \mid x=0] = \alpha + \beta \times 0 = \alpha\]
\(\beta\): the expected difference in y for observations one unit apart in x —
\[E[y \mid x=x_0+1] - E[y \mid x=x_0] = \big(\alpha + \beta(x_0+1)\big) - \big(\alpha + \beta x_0\big) = \beta\]

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
Precise language matters
Good ways to say what \(\beta\) means: “y is higher, on average, by \(\beta\) for observations with a one-unit higher x.”

Avoid “increases/decreases” — implies something changing over time. Avoid “effect” — implies causation. Neither is justified by a regression alone, on observational data.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 7

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
Regression on a binary x
Simplest case: x is 0/1 — like device (Laptop = 0, Phone = 1).

\(\alpha\) = average y when x = 0 (average reaction time on Laptop)
\(\beta\) = difference in average y between x = 1 and x = 0 (Phone minus Laptop)
\(\alpha + \beta\) = average y when x = 1 (average reaction time on Phone)
The regression line is just two points, connected


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 7

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text: The OLS estimator

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
The slope formula
\[\hat\beta = \frac{Cov[x,y]}{Var[x]}\]

The covariance between x and y, normalised by the variation in x
Measures the covariance relative to how spread out x is
That’s why it can be read as “difference in average y per unit difference in x”


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 7

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
The intercept formula
\[\hat\alpha = \bar y - \hat\beta \bar x\]

Average y, minus average x scaled by the slope we just found
A direct consequence: rearrange it and you get \(\bar y = \hat\alpha + \hat\beta \bar x\) — the fitted line always passes through the point \((\bar x, \bar y)\), the average of averages
Once \(\hat\beta\) is fixed, \(\hat\alpha\) isn’t a second independent choice — it’s whatever pins the line through that point


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 7

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
section: Var[x] is the same idea, applied to x alone
text:
Var[x] is the same idea, applied to x alone
\(Var[x] = Cov[x,x]\) — the identical rectangle idea, but pairing x with itself. Since a number times itself is never negative, every “rectangle” is the same colour: Var[x] is always positive, a pure measure of x’s own spread.

\(\hat\beta\) = (net signed area between x and y) ÷ (x’s own spread) — literally, how much x and y move together, relative to how much x moves on its own.

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
section: Why divide by Var[x] at all?

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
Why this particular line?
The residual for an observation is the gap between its actual y and what a candidate line predicts: \(y_i - (\alpha + \beta x_i)\). OLS chooses \(\hat\alpha, \hat\beta\) to minimise the sum of squared residuals:
\[\min_{\alpha,\beta} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \alpha - \beta x_i)^2\]

Solving this with calculus gives exactly the Cov/Var formula — we won’t derive it here (see the textbook, U7.1, if you’re curious). Instead, let’s watch it being the minimum.

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
section: Finding the bottom of the bowl

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
OLS is BLUE

Best Linear Unbiased Estimator — among every linear, unbiased way of estimating \(\beta\), OLS has the smallest variance. “Best” here means most precise, not most correct.


That guarantee isn’t unconditional — it holds only if a handful of assumptions about the data are true.

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
What has to be true?

Linearity — a straight line is a reasonable approximation
Independent observations — one observation’s error doesn’t leak into another’s
Homoskedasticity — the spread of residuals is roughly constant across the range of x, not fanning out or narrowing
No extreme influence — no single point is silently dragging the whole line

Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
section: Checking it on our own data

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
Interpolation vs. extrapolation

Using the fitted line: predict the mean reaction time for a finger length within the range we observed, then for one far outside it (e.g. 40mm or 110mm).


Interpolation — predicting within the range of x we’ve actually seen — is reasonably safe. Extrapolation — predicting beyond it — assumes the same straight-line pattern keeps holding somewhere we’ve never checked. For a screening tool HR might apply to any candidate, that assumption is doing a lot of unexamined work.

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text: How good is the fit?

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
R-squared
\[R^2 = \frac{Var[\hat y]}{Var[y]} = 1 - \frac{Var[e]}{Var[y]}\]
Decomposing the total variation in y into what the regression explains and what’s left over:
\[Var[y] = Var[\hat y] + Var[e]\]

\(R^2 = 0\): predicted values are just \(\bar y\) for everyone — the regression explains nothing
\(R^2 = 1\): every point sits exactly on the line
For simple regression: \(R^2 = (Corr[x,y])^2\) — a direct callback to Week 3

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
R-squared
You’ll also see this written as sums of squares rather than variances — same identity, just without dividing by \(n\). Software output (statsmodels, R, Excel) almost always uses this version:
\[\underbrace{\textstyle\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2}_{TSS} \;=\; \underbrace{\textstyle\sum(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2}_{ESS} \;+\; \underbrace{\textstyle\sum e_i^2}_{RSS} \qquad R^2 = \frac{ESS}{TSS} = 1 - \frac{RSS}{TSS}\]
TSS (total), ESS (explained), RSS (residual) — watch out, some textbooks swap the last two labels (calling the residual part “SSE”). Check what a given source means before trusting the letters alone.

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
Logs, revisited
Week 3’s online session logged reaction time because it’s skewed. In a regression, which variable you log changes what the slope means:



Model
Interpretation of β




Level–level
1-unit x → unit change in y


Log–level
1-unit x → % change in y


Level–log
1% change in x → unit change in y


Log–log
1% change in x → % change in y (elasticity)




Polynomials and splines can capture curvature a straight line misses — useful when prediction is the goal, but each added flexibility costs interpretability. Simpler is usually better; see the textbook for splines, we won’t build them live.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 7 & 8

text: Extreme values — and is it causal?

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
Influential observations
An observation is influential if including or excluding it noticeably moves the regression line — not the same as simply being an extreme value.

Same three-way decision as Week 1’s outliers: error → fix or drop; real but irrelevant to the question → drop, with a note; genuine feature of the process → keep. Try a transformation before ever dropping a point.

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
section: Watch one point move the line

title: Simple Regression: The OLS Estimator
text:
Is it causal?
The slope isn’t zero in our data. Gabor & Kézdi’s list of why, not mutually exclusive:

x causes y — longer fingers → faster reactions?
y causes x — implausible here, but always worth ruling out explicitly
A third variable causes both — hand size, age, or general dexterity could plausibly move both finger length and reaction time together


“Correlation doesn’t imply causation” undersells it. Better: we should not infer cause and effect from a comparison in observational data — not because the method is broken, but because nothing about it was designed to rule out the third alternative.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 7

section: Interpreting log models — the full picture
text:
Interpreting log models — the full picture
The table you previewed in Week 4, with the equation behind each row and the reasoning behind each interpretation:








Model
Equation
Interpretation of \(\hat\beta\)




Level–level
\(y^E = \alpha + \beta x\)
1-unit higher x → \(\hat\beta\)-unit higher y, on average


Log–level
\(\ln(y)^E = \alpha + \beta x\)
1-unit higher x → \(100\times\hat\beta\) % higher y, on average


Level–log
\(y^E = \alpha + \beta \ln(x)\)
1% higher x → \(\hat\beta/100\)-unit higher y, on average


Log–log
\(\ln(y)^E = \alpha + \beta \ln(x)\)
1% higher x → \(\hat\beta\)% higher y, on average — an elasticity




Which one to use is a substantive question first: is x likely to move y in multiplicative steps (percentages) or additive ones (fixed amounts)? Only then check whether the distributions agree.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 8

title: Model Problems & Inference
text:
When you can’t just log
Logging needs a strictly positive variable — never zero, never negative. Real data often isn’t:

Create a binary indicator, then log what’s left — e.g. “is wealth negative?” (0/1), “is wealth zero?” (0/1), and log the positive values, replacing the log with zero where it can’t be taken
Add a constant, \(\ln(x+1)\), if x is zero or positive — a common shortcut, but not principled; it’s least distorting when x tends to be large (there, \(\ln(x)\approx\ln(x+1)\) anyway)


Suppose a trial recorded exactly 0ms — a device timing glitch, not a real reaction. Would you drop it, indicator-and-log it, or use \(\ln(x+1)\)? What does your answer depend on?


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 8

title: Model Problems & Inference
text:
Ratios and per-capita measures
A common transform outside our own dataset: normalising a total by a size variable — GDP/capita, revenue/employee, sales/store.
\[\ln\left(\frac{GDP}{Population}\right) = \ln(GDP) - \ln(Population)\]

The log of a ratio is just the difference of the two logs — so a per-capita measure and its log both stay easy to interpret and combine with everything else you’ve learned about logs today.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 8

title: Model Problems & Inference
text:
Polynomials
A quadratic lets the slope change smoothly, without deciding where it bends:
\[y^E = \alpha + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2\]

\(\alpha\): average y when x = 0
\(\beta_1\) alone has no clean interpretation
\(\beta_2\): shape only — U-shaped (convex) if positive, inverted-U (concave) if negative
The slope at any point x is \(\beta_1 + 2\beta_2 x\) — it changes as x changes


A trade-off, not a downside: what this gives up in flexibility, it gains back in a coefficient you can actually explain.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 8

Which model actually fits better?

import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

section: The roadmap for choosing a functional form
text:
The roadmap for choosing a functional form

Check the distributions of y and x — skewed, long right tail?
Look at the shape — scatterplot or a non-parametric fit (bin-scatter, lowess)
Choose a transform to match what you see — and remember: not every variable can sensibly be logged or ratio’d
Compare models — if the results agree, that’s a robustness check; if they disagree sharply, find out why

text: Extreme values and influence

title: Model Problems & Inference
text:
Extreme value ≠ influential observation
An extreme value is just unusual on some variable. An influential observation is one whose presence or absence noticeably moves the regression line.

Every influential observation is extreme on something — but plenty of extreme values sit right near the line and barely matter. The two ideas get conflated; they shouldn’t be.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 8

title: Model Problems & Inference
section: What to do — and it depends which variable
text:
What to do — and it depends which variable

General rule: avoid dropping observations based on their y value. A genuinely strange outcome is still information — dropping it because it’s inconvenient biases what’s left
Dropping on x can be more defensible — if that x value is atypical for the question you’re asking
But often the opposite is true: extreme x values are the most informative ones, since they’re where you see the most variation in the pattern
Always try a transformation before ever dropping a point


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 8

title: Model Problems & Inference
Model Problems & Inference
text: Measurement error

title: Model Problems & Inference
text:
Nothing here is measured exactly
Every number in our dataset carries some noise:

Reaction time — self-timed by students on their own devices, with browser and reflex lag
Finger length — self-measured with a ruler, to the nearest millimetre, by hand


This isn’t a flaw specific to our exercise — almost all data in business and economics is measured with error. The question isn’t whether it exists, but what it does to \(\hat\beta\).

title: Model Problems & Inference
text:
Classical measurement error
A measured variable equals its true value plus noise: \(x = x^* + e\)

Classical measurement error: (1) averages to zero — it doesn’t shift the variable’s mean — and (2) is independent of everything else in the model, including the true value itself.


Recording slips, rounding, reflex-timing lag — plausibly classical. A systematically miscalibrated ruler would not be.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 8

title: Model Problems & Inference
section: Noise in y doesn’t bias the slope
text:
Noise in y doesn’t bias the slope
If only the dependent variable is measured with classical error, \(y = y^* + e\):
\[\hat\beta = \frac{Cov[y,x]}{Var[x]} = \frac{Cov[y^*+e,\ x]}{Var[x]} = \frac{Cov[y^*,x] + Cov[e,x]}{Var[x]} = \frac{Cov[y^*,x]}{Var[x]} = \hat\beta^*\]

\(Cov[e,x]=0\) by the classical assumption, so it drops straight out. Noisy y makes the fit worse — more scatter around the line — but it doesn’t move \(\hat\beta\) on average.

title: Model Problems & Inference
section: Noise in x does — attenuation bias
text:
Noise in x does — attenuation bias
If the explanatory variable is measured with classical error, \(x = x^*+e\), the noise inflates \(Var[x]\) itself:
\[\hat\beta = \hat\beta^* \times \frac{Var[x^*]}{Var[x^*] + Var[e]}\]

That fraction is always less than one — so \(\hat\beta\) is always pulled toward zero, never away from it. This is attenuation bias. The noisier x is relative to its real variation, the flatter the estimated slope looks, regardless of the true relationship.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 8

title: Model Problems & Inference
Model Problems & Inference
text:
Noise-to-signal ratio
\[\text{noise-to-signal} = \frac{Var[e]}{Var[x^*]}\]

Low ratio — recording is careful, or the variable is an aggregate over a large sample. Often safe to ignore
High ratio — the noise added is large relative to the real spread in x. Worth taking seriously, and worth being upfront about in any write-up


You can rarely eliminate measurement error. You can almost always say something honest about its likely direction — and for x, that direction is always toward zero.

title: Model Problems & Inference
section: How sure are we about β̂?
text:
How sure are we about β̂?
Week 2 built a confidence interval for a mean. Exactly the same logic now applies to a slope:
\[CI(\hat\beta)_{95\%} = \left[\hat\beta - 2\,SE(\hat\beta),\ \ \hat\beta + 2\,SE(\hat\beta)\right]\]

Same idea as \(CI(\bar x) = \bar x \pm 2\,SE(\bar x)\) from Week 2 — a plausible range for the true slope, built from how much \(\hat\beta\) would bounce around across repeated samples.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 9

title: Model Problems & Inference
text:
Where SE(β̂) comes from
\[SE(\hat\beta) = \frac{Std[e]}{\sqrt{n}\cdot Std[x]}\]
SE(β̂) is smaller — the estimate more precise — when:

Std[e] is small — the line fits well, little left-over scatter
Std[x] is large — x varies a lot in the data
n is large — more observations


Notice: this is the same \(Std[e]\) and \(Std[x]\) from Week 4’s slope formula. Precision and the estimate itself come from the same ingredients.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 9

Model Problems & Inference
section: Testing if β is really zero
text:
Testing if β is really zero
\[H_0: \beta_{true} = 0 \qquad H_A: \beta_{true} \neq 0 \qquad\qquad t = \frac{\hat\beta}{SE(\hat\beta)}\]

\(t \approx 2\) corresponds to the 95% CI boundary — the same threshold, from a different angle
A coefficient is “statistically significant” if its CI doesn’t contain zero — most commonly at the 5% level (\(p<0.05\))


This is the exact same t-statistic logic as Week 2’s tea test — just applied to a slope instead of a mean difference.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 9

title: Model Problems & Inference
text:
Two different questions about prediction

Confidence interval for the predicted value — where do we expect the average y to be, for a given x? Uncertainty about \(\hat\alpha\) and \(\hat\beta\) only
Prediction interval — where do we expect one particular y to actually land, for a given x? Adds the extra spread of individual observations around their own average


The CI narrows toward zero as n grows. The PI never does — no amount of data removes the fact that individuals vary around the average.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 9

title: Model Problems, in Real Data
text:
What each slope actually says

Level–level: hotels 1 mile farther out are $14 cheaper, on average
Log–level: hotels 1 mile farther out are 13% cheaper, on average
Level–log: hotels 10% farther out are $2.48 cheaper, on average
Log–log: hotels 10% farther out are 2.2% cheaper, on average — an elasticity


Four different numbers, from the same underlying data. None of them is “wrong” — they answer four subtly different questions.

title: Model Problems, in Real Data
section: Which one should you actually use?
text:
Which one should you actually use?
Substantive reasoning comes first. It depends on the goal:

Chasing an absolute good deal for one night? Dollar differences are what matter — level price
Comparing across seasons where inflation and demand move prices proportionately? Percentage differences travel better — log price
Distance itself is usually more natural in miles than in relative terms, for this particular question


Notice the R² rises every step down that table, from 0.157 to 0.334. Is log-log simply the “best” model? What’s wrong with reading it that way?

title: Model Problems, in Real Data
text:
The R² trap
You cannot compare R² across regressions with different dependent variables. Level-price and log-price R² are fit measures in different units — one describes variation in dollars, the other in log-dollars. A higher number doesn’t mean a better model.

Valid comparisons: level-level vs. level-log (both explain price); log-level vs. log-log (both explain ln(price)). Within each pair, the higher R² is meaningful. Across pairs, it isn’t.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 8

title: Model Problems, in Real Data
section: Splines: full flexibility, at a cost
text: Splines: full flexibility, at a cost

title: Model Problems, in Real Data
text:
Piecewise linear splines
A spline breaks x into intervals at chosen knots, and fits a separate line segment in each — connected at the knots, but each segment free to have its own slope.
\[y^E = (\alpha_1+\beta_1 x)\ [x<k_1] + (\alpha_2+\beta_2 x)\ [k_1\le x\le k_2] + \dots\]

Each \(\beta\) is interpretable on its own — the slope within that segment only
Handles any shape, including non-monotonic patterns a quadratic can’t
The cost: you choose the number of knots and where they go — no longer automatic


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 8

Model Problems, in Real Data
text: When measurement error isn’t classical

title: Model Problems, in Real Data
section: Real noise is rarely this polite
text:
Real noise is rarely this polite
The workshop’s attenuation-bias result relied on classical measurement error: zero mean, independent of everything else. In practice:

Error may not average to zero — a scale that’s consistently a little heavy, a ruler with a worn end
Error may be correlated with the true value or other variables — people who feel unwell might round symptoms in a particular direction, not randomly


Our finger-length measurements were self-reported with a ruler. Can you think of a way that error could be non-classical, rather than just noisy?


Without classical error, the “always toward zero” result no longer holds — bias could go either way. The fix isn’t a formula; it’s redesigning how the variable is measured.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 8

section: Hotel ratings: a noisier x for some hotels than others
text:
Hotel ratings: a noisier x for some hotels than others
Price comparison sites publish an average customer rating per hotel — but that average is noisier when it’s based on fewer reviews.

Few ratings (< 100 reviews): 77 hotels, ~57 ratings each, rating SD = 0.42
Many ratings (> 200 reviews): 72 hotels, ~417 ratings each, rating SD = 0.26


If classical measurement error is at work, the few-ratings group has the noisier x — and the workshop’s result predicts exactly one thing: a flatter slope for that group.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 8

Gabor & Kézdi leave this open deliberately. Given what you now know about attenuation bias — would you drop the few-ratings hotels, keep them and just report the likely direction of bias, or something else? What would you tell a client who only saw the few-ratings estimate?

Multiple regression
Finger length alone barely moved the needle. What if device or caffeine matter too — and are tangled up with finger length itself?

title: Multiple Regression
section: One x at a time was never the whole story
text:
One x at a time was never the whole story

HR has separate regressions: reaction time on finger length, reaction time on device. Someone asks: which one actually matters?


Naive answer: run each regression separately, compare the slopes, done.
Why it’s not that simple: if finger length and device happen to be correlated in our sample — say, one device tends to attract a particular hand-size group — each regression is silently absorbing some of the other variable’s effect. We can’t tell which x is doing the work until we ask both questions at once.

title: Multiple Regression
text: Why more than one x?

title: Multiple Regression
section: Three reasons to add a second x
text:
Three reasons to add a second x

Broader patterns — plain exploratory work, understanding the data more fully
Closer to comparing similar observations — holding one variable fixed while looking at another gets nearer to ceteris paribus, “all else equal”
Better prediction — more of the variation in y gets explained


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Two x variables
\[y^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2\]

\(\beta_1\): the difference in average y across observations that differ in \(x_1\) but share the same \(x_2\)
\(\beta_2\): the same idea, the other way round
We can now compare observations that are similar in one explanatory variable, to isolate what the other one is doing


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Reading real output
From here on, every regression we show comes with the code that produced it. We’ll assume the data’s already clean — the focus is the model-fitting call and how to read what comes back.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

model = smf.ols('reaction_time_ms ~ finger_mm + device', data=df).fit(cov_type='HC1')
print(model.summary())

cov_type='HC1' — heteroskedasticity-robust SE, the Week 5 default, carried forward as standard practice.

title: Multiple Regression
text: Omitted variable bias

title: Multiple Regression
section: Comparing the simple and multiple slope
text:
Comparing the simple and multiple slope
\[y^E = \alpha + \beta x_1 \qquad\qquad y^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2\]
An intermediate step — regress \(x_2\) on \(x_1\) itself, slope \(\delta\):
\[x_2^E = \gamma + \delta x_1\]

Substituting back in gives a precise relationship between the two versions of the \(x_1\) slope:
\[\beta - \beta_1 = \delta\beta_2\]


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Omitted variable bias, named
\[\beta - \beta_1 = \delta\beta_2\]

This gap is the omitted variable bias (OVB)
If you care about \(\beta_1\), the simple regression \(y^E=\alpha+\beta x_1\) is the wrong regression — it omits \(x_2\)
The bias is exactly zero only if \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are uncorrelated (\(\delta=0\)), or \(x_2\) has no effect on y in the full model (\(\beta_2=0\))


Neither condition is something you can assume — it has to be checked, or reasoned about.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
section: Worked example: beer sales and price
text:
Worked example: beer sales and price

A scenario where we can control the truth: monthly change in our log price (\(x_1\)) and a competitor’s log price (\(x_2\)) tend to move together, both driving change in log sales (y). Simulate it, and check the OVB formula holds exactly.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
competitor_price = rng.normal(0, 2.0, 300)
our_price        = 0.8 * competitor_price + rng.normal(0, 1.2, 300)   # correlated with competitor's
sales            = -3*our_price + 3*competitor_price + rng.normal(0, 2.5, 300)  # true betas: -3, +3
df = pd.DataFrame({'sales': sales, 'our_price': our_price, 'competitor_price': competitor_price})

simple = smf.ols('sales ~ our_price', data=df).fit()
multi  = smf.ols('sales ~ our_price + competitor_price', data=df).fit()
aux    = smf.ols('competitor_price ~ our_price', data=df).fit()   # x2 on x1, per the formula above

beta (simple)     = -0.949beta1 (multiple)  = -3.273beta2 (multiple)  = 3.125delta (x2 on x1)  = 0.744



beta − beta1 = 2.3244    delta×beta2 = 2.3244

The two sides match exactly — \(\hat\beta-\hat\beta_1\) and \(\hat\delta\hat\beta_2\) are the same calculation, done two different ways. And since we built this dataset ourselves, we know the simple regression really is biased: the true effect of our own price is \(-3\), but \(\hat\beta\) lands nowhere near it — because it’s silently absorbing the competitor-price effect too, through the correlation between the two.

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Language: conditioning, controlling, confounding

We measure differences in y by \(x_1\), conditional on \(x_2\) — or controlling for \(x_2\)
When a variable that belongs in the model is left out, it’s an omitted variable
If it’s correlated with both \(x_1\) and y, it’s a confounder — the slope on \(x_1\) is confounded


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
text: Multicollinearity — a different problem

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multicollinearity, defined

Multicollinearity: two or more explanatory variables in the same regression are strongly correlated with each other.


It does not bias any coefficient — β̂ is still right, on average
It inflates the standard errors — β̂ becomes imprecise, harder to pin down
Intuition: if \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) move together almost every time, there’s barely any data where one is high and the other is low — and that’s exactly the comparison OLS needs to estimate their separate slopes


Contrast with Section B: OVB is about what’s missing from the model. Multicollinearity is about what’s already in it, just tangled together.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
section: Where the standard error comes from
text:
Where the standard error comes from
\[SE(\hat\beta_1) = \frac{Std[e]}{\sqrt{n}\cdot Std[x_1]\cdot\sqrt{1-R_1^2}}\]

Same ingredients as Week 5’s simple-regression SE — fit, spread of \(x_1\), sample size
New: \(R_1^2\) — the R² from regressing \(x_1\) on \(x_2\) (and any other x’s). The more \(x_1\) is explained by the other regressors, the bigger this term, the bigger the SE


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Perfect vs. imperfect collinearity

Perfect collinearity — \(x_1\) is an exact linear function of \(x_2\). Coefficients literally can’t be calculated; software drops one variable for you
Multicollinearity — strong but imperfect correlation between explanatory variables. Coefficients and SEs can still be computed — but the SEs may be large


Intuition: multicollinearity means there aren’t many observations that differ in \(x_1\) while staying similar in \(x_2\) — so there’s little clean information left to estimate \(\beta_1\) precisely.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
Multiple Regression
text:
Naming it: VIF
Software usually calls this number the Variance Inflation Factor:
\[VIF_k = \frac{1}{1-R_k^2}\]

The exact same \(R_k^2\) from two slides ago — just flipped into one number per variable
Common rule of thumb: VIF > 10 flags a real problem (some use a stricter >5)
One line in statsmodels: variance_inflation_factor(X, k)

title: Multiple Regression
Multiple Regression
text:
The VIF trap

A high VIF does not mean “drop this variable.” If it’s a genuine confounder, dropping it to fix a precision problem reintroduces the bias problem from Section B — often a worse trade.


The honest response to a high VIF is usually: report it, keep the variable if the causal story needs it, and be upfront that the estimate is imprecise. VIF is a diagnostic, not a decision rule.

title: Multiple Regression
section: What to actually do about it
text:
What to actually do about it

Look at pairwise correlations (or a correlation heatmap) early, before modelling
Drop one of a highly correlated pair, or combine them (average, or a z-score index)
Mostly a small-sample problem — hundreds to a few thousand observations
With many x’s: check \(R_k^2\) for each variable regressed on all the others; drop if very high


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
text:
The distinction that matters









Omitted variable bias
Multicollinearity




What it is
Leaving out a variable that belongs in the model
Including two variables that are strongly correlated


What it breaks
The point estimate itself — wrong on average
Precision — the estimate is right on average, just noisy


Does more data fix it?
No. Same bias at any sample size
Yes. More data narrows the SE back down


Direction known?
Depends on \(\delta\) and \(\beta_2\) — could go either way
N/A — SE inflates, doesn’t shift the estimate




Confusing these two is the single most common mistake in reading regression output. One is a bias problem you fix by adding the right variable. The other is a precision problem you sometimes fix by removing one.

title: Multiple Regression
text: Testing more than one coefficient

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Individual coefficients — same as before
Each \(\hat\beta_k\) gets its own CI and t-test, exactly as in Week 5:
\[CI(\hat\beta_k)_{95\%} = \hat\beta_k \pm 2\,SE(\hat\beta_k) \qquad\qquad t=\frac{\hat\beta_k}{SE(\hat\beta_k)}\]
The only change is where \(SE(\hat\beta_k)\) comes from — the formula with the \(\sqrt{1-R_k^2}\) term from Section C.

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Testing several coefficients together
Sometimes the question isn’t about one coefficient, but a group of them — e.g. “are all the geography dummies jointly zero?”

The F-test answers this. Individually, none of the coefficients might be statistically distinguishable from zero — but jointly, they might still be.


The global F-test — are all slope coefficients zero? — is reported by default in most software. Gabor & Kézdi’s own advice: don’t lean on it too heavily. R² tells you almost the same thing, more simply, for that particular question.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
text:
The full output, F-test included
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

model = smf.ols('reaction_time_ms ~ finger_mm + device + caffeine', data=df).fit(cov_type='HC1')
print(model.summary())

Prob (F-statistic) = 0.115 — can’t reject that all three slopes are jointly zero. 200 rows looks like a lot, but it’s really only 20 students × 10 repeated trials each — since finger length, device, and caffeine don’t change trial-to-trial, the coefficients are identical to what you’d get averaging each student down to one row first. Same multicollinearity warning as Section C, flagged again at the bottom.

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Presenting it as a table
Pull the real numbers straight off the fitted model into a small results table, then let pandas do the formatting:
def stars(p):
    return "***" if p < 0.01 else "**" if p < 0.05 else "*" if p < 0.1 else ""

results_df = pd.DataFrame(
    [{"Variable": label,
      "Coefficient": f"{model.params[name]:.2f}{stars(model.pvalues[name])}",
      "Std. Error": f"({model.bse[name]:.2f})"}
     for name, label in labels.items()]
    + [{"Variable": "N", "Coefficient": str(int(model.nobs)), "Std. Error": ""},
       {"Variable": "R²", "Coefficient": f"{model.rsquared:.3f}", "Std. Error": ""}]
)
print(results_df.to_markdown(index=False))

to_markdown() is a built-in pandas method — no LaTeX, no extra formatting library beyond tabulate (one pip install away).

text: Categorical variables, properly

title: Multiple Regression
text:
k categories, k − 1 dummies
A categorical x with values low/medium/high becomes two binary variables — one category left out as the reference:
\[y^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{medium} + \beta_2 x_{high}\]

\(\beta_0\) — average y in the reference category (low)
\(\beta_1\) — difference between medium and low
\(\beta_2\) — difference between high and low


Include all k dummies (no reference left out) and you get the dummy variable trap — perfect collinearity with the intercept, and the model can’t be estimated.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Choosing a reference category

Substantive guide — pick whatever you naturally want everything else compared to (the home market, the base product, the lowest tier)
Statistical guide — pick a category with plenty of observations. A thin reference category means every comparison against it inherits a large SE


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

section: Interactions: different slopes for different groups
text: Interactions: different slopes for different groups

title: Multiple Regression
section: When the pattern itself varies by group
text:
When the pattern itself varies by group
An interaction asks: does the relationship between y and \(x_1\) differ depending on a second variable, D? D is sometimes called a moderator.

Examples: does customer rating relate to hotel price differently by star category? Does a drug’s effect vary with patient age? Does the finger-length/reaction-time pattern differ by device?


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
text:
The structural model
\[y^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 D + \beta_3\,(x_1 \times D)\]

When \(D=0\): \(y^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1\) — intercept \(\beta_0\), slope \(\beta_1\)
When \(D=1\): \(y^E = (\beta_0+\beta_2) + (\beta_1+\beta_3)\,x_1\) — intercept shifts by \(\beta_2\), slope shifts by \(\beta_3\)


\(\beta_3\) is the answer to the interaction question — literally the difference in slopes between the two groups. It gets its own SE, its own t-stat, its own CI, exactly like any other coefficient.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

section: Our own data hits its limit
text:
Our own data hits its limit

20 students, 200 trials — even a real interaction would be hard to detect at this scale, and a weak or noisy one is essentially invisible against sampling noise this size.


To actually see an interaction at work, we need a dataset with enough power to show one. Back to the CPS earnings data from Section E — 18,241 people, real signal, real stakes.

section: Real case study: does the gender pay gap change with age?

title: Multiple Regression
section: Does a near-zero coefficient mean no gap?
text:
Does a near-zero coefficient mean no gap?

female = −0.036, not even statistically distinguishable from zero (p ≈ 0.30). Does this mean the gender gap has disappeared? What does female × age = −0.003, strongly significant, tell you that the female coefficient alone doesn’t?


Reread the structural model: at \(D=1\) (female), the slope on age is \(\beta_1+\beta_3\), not \(\beta_1\). The “female” coefficient alone only describes the gap at age zero — a meaningless, never-observed point. The real story is in \(\beta_3\).

title: Multiple Regression
Multiple Regression
text: Is it (more) causal?

title: Multiple Regression
section: Ceteris paribus is a destination, not a guarantee
text:
Ceteris paribus is a destination, not a guarantee
Conditioning on more variables gets us closer to comparing “apples to apples,” even in observational data. But:

Ceteris paribus means conditioning on every relevant confounder
A regression can only condition on what’s actually in the dataset, measured the way it happens to be measured
Conditioning on everything is impossible in general. Multiple regression is hardly ever truly ceteris paribus


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Not every correlated variable belongs

Question: to see how TV advertising affects sales, should you control for how many people viewed the advert?


No. Fewer views is part of why less advertising hurts sales — it’s not a confounder, it’s a step in the causal chain itself. Controlling for it would control away the very thing you’re trying to measure.


These are sometimes called bad controls. Telling a genuine confounder from a bad control by eye is genuinely hard — we’ll get a proper diagram for reasoning about this in Week 9.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Language, still
Even with five variables conditioned on, a regression is still a comparison of conditional means — not a randomized experiment.

Same rule as Week 4: avoid “effect,” avoid “increases/decreases,” in observational data. “Higher finger length is associated with a difference of X ms, holding device and caffeine fixed” is honest. “Finger length affects reaction time” is not — not yet.

title: Multiple Regression
text: Prediction, overfitting, and choosing variables

title: Multiple Regression
text:
The ŷ–y plot
\[\hat y = \hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_1+\hat\beta_2x_2+\dots\]
A scatterplot of \(\hat y\) (predicted) against actual y, with the 45° line:

Points right of the line: overpredicted
Points left of the line: underpredicted
More informative than R² alone — it shows where the model struggles, not just how much

title: Multiple Regression
Multiple Regression
text:
Overfitting and choosing variables

R² mechanically rises every time you add a variable — even pure noise. It can never fall
Overfitting: capturing patterns specific to this dataset that won’t hold up elsewhere
Purpose changes the rule: for a causal question, keep confounders that matter for comparison even if imprecise; for prediction, value simplicity and generalisability over fit


Rough sample-size guide (Gabor & Kézdi): 20–40 observations supports about 1–2 variables; 50–100 supports 2–4; a few hundred supports 5–10; a few thousand can support dozens, including dummies and interactions. Formal criteria like BIC penalise added variables directly — more in Week 10.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Summary

Multiple regression is a linear model with several x’s, letting us compare observations that are similar in one variable while differing in another
Omitted variable bias (leaving out a relevant, correlated variable) and multicollinearity (including two correlated variables) are opposite problems — bias vs. precision — and the fix for one is not the fix for the other
It gets us closer to a causal comparison, never all the way there
More variables always raises R² — that’s not the same as a better model

Set up

2014 census data

Age between 15 to 65
Self-employed excluded as earning are difficult to measure

Employees with a graduate degree

Let’s include age as well:
\[\ln w^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 female + \beta_2 age \] We can also calculate the correlation between female and age: \[ age^E = \gamma + \delta female\]

Among graduate-degree holders, the proportion of women drops noticeably after age 45, and again after 55 — men’s age distribution stays close to uniform from 30 to 55.

Interactions and non-linearities together
Let’s consider two models
\[ \ln w^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 age + \beta_2 female + \beta_3 female \times age \]
and adding age as non-linear
\[ \ln w^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 age + \beta_2 age^2 + \beta_3 age^3 + \beta_4 age^4 \\ + \beta_5 female + \beta_6 female \times age + \beta_7 female \times age ^2 \\ + \beta_8 female \times age^3 + \beta_9 female \times age^4 \]

title: Multiple Regression, Worked Through
text:
Interactions and non-linearities together
Running the fully flexible version — 4th-order polynomial in age, interacted with gender — reveals the real pattern:

The gap is around 10–8% between ages 25–30
Rises to 17% by 40, and 22% by 50
Tapers slightly after 60 (19%)


A single “female” coefficient could never have told this story. The gap isn’t a fixed number — it grows through most of a career and only the full interacted, non-linear model shows that shape.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression, Worked Through
text:
Predicting the gap by age
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

age_grid = np.linspace(25, 65, 50)

def predict_band(model, ages, female):
    X = pd.DataFrame({'age': ages, 'female': female})
    return model.get_prediction(X).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), sharey=True)
panels = [(axes[0], inter, 'Linear interaction'),
          (axes[1], full, '4th-order polynomial interaction')]

for ax, model, title in panels:
    for female, color, label in [(0, '#2d6a4f', 'Male'), (1, '#457b9d', 'Female')]:
        band = predict_band(model, age_grid, female)
        ax.plot(age_grid, band['mean'], color=color, label=label)
        ax.fill_between(age_grid, band['mean_ci_lower'], band['mean_ci_upper'], color=color, alpha=0.15)
    ax.set_xlabel('Age (years)')
    ax.set_title(title)

axes[0].set_ylabel('ln(earnings per hour)')
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

title: Multiple Regression, Worked Through
text:
The gap by age, plotted


Both panels show predicted ln(earnings) by age and gender, with 95% confidence bands. The linear-interaction panel forces the gap to widen at a constant rate; the polynomial panel lets it curve — women’s predicted earnings flatten and dip after around 45, exactly where the age-distribution wrinkle showed fewer women in the data to estimate from precisely.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: Multiple Regression, Worked Through
text:
What we still can’t say

Multiple regression got us closer to a fair comparison — same age, same education
It cannot rule out that broader gender inequality (career interruptions, occupational sorting, negotiation norms) drives part of what’s left
We can’t prove how much of the remaining gap is labour-market discrimination specifically — there’s too much unmeasured heterogeneity
And we haven’t ruled out selection or bad conditioning variables either


This is the honest ceiling of conditioning on observables. Getting further needs a different kind of design — which is where the module goes from Week 9 onward.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
section: Does smoking pose a health risk?
text:
Does smoking pose a health risk?

Business question: among people who are currently healthy, does smoking meaningfully raise the chance their health declines over the next few years — once other differences between smokers and non-smokers are accounted for?


We have real data: 3,112 people aged 50–60, healthy at the start, tracked four years later. stayshealthy is 1 if still healthy, 0 if not.

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
text:
The naive answer
Naive answer: compare the fraction of smokers who stayed healthy to the fraction of non-smokers who did. Done.

Why it’s not that simple: smokers and non-smokers differ in plenty of other ways — age, exercise, income, education — exactly the confounding problem from Week 6. And the outcome itself is different from anything we’ve modelled so far: it only ever takes the value 0 or 1.

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
text:
What we need

A regression framework built for a 0/1 outcome, not just a workaround bolted onto OLS
A way to interpret coefficients when the outcome is a probability, not a quantity
A sense of whether the model is actually any good, when it can never predict a 0 or a 1 exactly

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
section: Binary outcomes and the latent variable
text: Binary outcomes and the latent variable

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
text:
What’s different about a 0/1 y

The expected value of a binary variable is a probability: \(E[y] = P[y=1]\)
Frequency and probability become the same idea: 25% of cases having \(y=1\) is the same statement as a 25% chance of the event
So “modelling y” here really means modelling a probability

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
section: Where does the 0/1 actually come from?
text:
Where does the 0/1 actually come from?
Think about what “staying healthy” really is — it isn’t binary at all. Health is a continuum: some people are robustly healthy, some are fragile but not yet ill, some are already declining.

There’s an unobserved, continuous latent variable — call it \(y^*\) — representing that underlying health trajectory. We don’t observe \(y^*\) directly. We only observe whether it crossed a threshold:
\[y = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } y^* > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } y^* \le 0 \end{cases}\]

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
text:
Why the latent variable matters

If \(y^*\) is linear in \(x\) plus some random error — \(y^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + e\) — then:
\[P[y=1|x] = P[y^*>0|x] = P[e > -(\beta_0+\beta_1 x_1+\dots)]\]


This is a probability, so it has to come from the distribution of that error term \(e\) — specifically, its cumulative distribution function.

Assume \(e\) is logistic → you get the logit model
Assume \(e\) is normal → you get the probit model
Ignore this altogether and model \(y\) directly with a straight line → you get the linear probability model

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
section: One family: the Generalized Linear Model
text:
One family: the Generalized Linear Model
Every model this session share the same three-part structure:

A linear predictor: \(\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots\)
A link function connecting \(\eta\) to \(E[y|x]\)
A distributional assumption for \(y\)


This is the Generalized Linear Model (GLM). Logit and probit aren’t a separate technique from what you already know — and neither, in a moment, will Poisson be.

text: The linear probability model

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
text:
LPM — the simplest option
\[y^P = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots\]

\(y^P\) denotes \(P[y=1|x_1,x_2,\dots]\)
Just OLS, with a binary y — everything from Weeks 4–6 still applies: logs, splines, interactions, robust SEs
Heteroskedasticity-robust SEs are essential — LPM residuals are mechanically heteroskedastic


Not just usually — mechanically: y is Bernoulli, so \(Var[y\mid x] = y^P(1-y^P)\). The residual variance is a direct function of the predicted probability itself, which changes with x by construction. There is no version of this model where the residual spread is constant — homoskedasticity isn’t just unlikely here, it’s ruled out by what a binary variable is.
