text:
The bigger problem with LPM
We often want to use our model to predict outcomes. Let’s do that here.
Predicted values - \(\hat{y}^P\) - may cause problems.
lpm_pred = model.predict(df)
lpm_pred.describe()

html`<div style="font-family:sans-serif;">
  <p>Predicted probabilities in this model range from <b>${lpm_pred_min}</b> to <b>${lpm_pred_max}</b>, across <b>${results_n}</b> observations.</p>
  <p><b>${n_above_1}</b> observation${n_above_1 === 1 ? '' : 's'} — out of ${results_n} — get${n_above_1 === 1 ? 's' : ''} a predicted probability above 1.</p>
</div>`







One observation gets a predicted probability above 1 — a meaningless value for something that’s supposed to be a probability. Nothing in the LPM’s structure stops this from happening.


For inference — uncovering patterns of association — this is rarely a big problem. For prediction, it’s a real one: you can’t tell a client their chance of an outcome is 104%.

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
text: Logit and probit

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
text:
Fixing the range problem
Recall the latent-variable story: \(P[y=1|x]\) has to come from a genuine probability distribution’s CDF — which is bounded between 0 and 1 by construction.

Logit: assumes \(e\) is logistic → link function is the logistic function \(\Lambda(z) = \dfrac{\exp(z)}{1+\exp(z)}\)
Probit: assumes \(e\) is normal → link function is \(\Phi(z)\), the standard normal CDF
Both are increasing, S-shaped, and strictly between 0 and 1

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes

text:
Why raw coefficients stop working

LPM’s slope is constant — a one-unit change in \(x\) shifts \(y^P\) by the same amount everywhere
Logit and probit’s slope changes depending on where you are on the S-curve — steepest at \(y^P=0.5\), flattest near 0 or 1
Direct consequence: you cannot read raw logit/probit coefficients the way you read an LPM or OLS coefficient

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
text:
Marginal effects — the fix
The average marginal effect (AME) is the average, across everyone in the data, of how much \(y^P\) changes for a one-unit change in \(x\).


Computed via numerical derivatives, not by hand — that’s what the marginaleffects package is for
Has the exact same interpretation as an LPM coefficient


import marginaleffects as me

logit_model = smf.logit("stayshealthy ~ smoking + ever_smoked + female + age + eduyears + income10 + bmi + exerc", data=df).fit()
ame = me.avg_slopes(logit_model)

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
section: Why R² doesn’t quite work here
text:
Why R² doesn’t quite work here

A probability model will never predict exactly 0 or exactly 1 — so it can never “perfectly” fit a 0/1 outcome the way OLS can fit a continuous one
\(R^2\) can still be computed, but it no longer carries the same “share of variance explained” meaning
We need measures built for probability outcomes

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes
text:
Three purpose-built measures

Brier score — mean squared distance between predicted probability and actual outcome. Smaller is better.
Pseudo R² (McFadden’s) — ratio of the model’s log-likelihood to an intercept-only model’s. Works for logit/probit, not LPM (no likelihood function there).
Log-loss — a negative number; closer to zero is better.

title: GLMs — Binary Outcomes

text:
Calibration — a sharper question
Unbiasedness asks: is the model right on average? Calibration asks something stricter: is it right at every predicted probability level?

Take everyone predicted around a 30% chance of staying healthy. If roughly 30% of them actually did, the model is well calibrated there. Do this across the whole range of predictions — that’s a calibration curve.

text:
Real calibration curve
df["pred_logit"] = logit_model.predict(df)
df["decile"] = pd.qcut(df["pred_logit"], 10, labels=False)

calib = (df.groupby("decile")
           .agg(pred=("pred_logit", "mean"), actual=("stayshealthy", "mean"))
           .reset_index())



Plot.plot({
  width: 500, height: 500,
  x: {label: "Predicted probability", domain: [0,1]},
  y: {label: "Actual outcome rate", domain: [0,1]},

    Plot.line([{x:0,y:0},{x:1,y:1}], {x:"x", y:"y", stroke:"#ccc", strokeDasharray:"4,4"}),
    Plot.line(calibration_data, {x:"pred", y:"actual", stroke:"#2d6a4f", strokeWidth:2}),

  ]
})









Deciles of predicted probability from the logit model, against the actual fraction who stayed healthy in each decile. Close to the diagonal — well calibrated, not just unbiased on average.

A binary y is really a probability to be modelled — the latent-variable story explains why link functions exist, not just that they do
LPM is OLS with a 0/1 y — simple, but predicted probabilities can fall outside [0,1]

title: GLMs — Count Outcomes
text:
Count outcomes
The workshop covered a 0/1 outcome. What about an outcome that can be 0, 1, 2, 3… with no natural ceiling?

title: GLMs — Count Outcomes
text:
How many bikes today?

Business question: a bike-share operator needs to plan how many bikes to have available each day. Rentals range from 22 on the worst day to 8,714 on the best — driven by weather, season, and whether it’s a working day.


This is real UCI data: 731 days, daily rental counts (cnt), temperature, humidity, windspeed, season, and working-day status.

title: GLMs — Count Outcomes
text:
Same logic, new distribution
Everything from the workshop still applies — a link function connects a linear index to the outcome, and raw coefficients aren’t directly interpretable.


Binary y: link function keeps predictions between 0 and 1 (logistic or normal CDF)
Count y: link function needs to keep predictions non-negative — no upper bound needed, but never below zero
The natural choice: \(E[y|x] = \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots)\) — the log link

title: GLMs — Count Outcomes
text:
Poisson regression
\[\ln(E[y|x]) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots\]

The Poisson distribution is the standard choice for count data — same role here as the logistic/normal assumption played for binary y
Fit by maximum likelihood, same idea as logit and probit
Because of the log link, coefficients are additive on the log scale, multiplicative on the count scale

title: GLMs — Count Outcomes
section: Interpreting via the incidence rate ratio
text:
Interpreting via the incidence rate ratio
Exponentiating a coefficient converts it into an incidence rate ratio (IRR):
\[IRR = \exp(\beta_1)\]

A one-unit increase in \(x_1\) multiplies the expected count by \(IRR\) — not adds to it. Same underlying logic as an odds ratio from logit, just for counts instead of binary outcomes.



\(IRR > 1\): expected count goes up
\(IRR < 1\): expected count goes down
\(IRR = 1\): no effect

text:
Fitting it, in code
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

poisson_model = smf.glm(
    "cnt ~ temp_c + workingday + C(season_name) + windspeed + hum",
    data=df,
    family=sm.families.Poisson()
).fit()

irr = np.exp(poisson_model.params)

section: Is Poisson actually a good fit here?
text: Is Poisson actually a good fit here?

title: GLMs — Count Outcomes
text:
Poisson’s hidden assumption
Poisson regression assumes equidispersion: the variance of \(y\) equals its mean, \(Var(y|x) = E(y|x)\).

On this data:

Mean daily rentals: 
Variance: 
Ratio: ×



The variance is nowhere close to the mean — this is severe overdispersion. Daily rental counts are the sum of thousands of individual decisions, which naturally vary far more than a simple Poisson process would predict.

title: GLMs — Count Outcomes
text:
Why this matters
Fitting a plain Poisson model when the data is this overdispersed doesn’t just look untidy — it makes every standard error too small, which makes every result look more certain than it actually is.

We need a model that keeps the same log link and the same IRR interpretation, but doesn’t force variance to equal the mean.

title: GLMs — Count Outcomes
text:
Negative binomial — the fix

Same log link, same IRR interpretation — nothing about reading the model changes
Adds one extra parameter, α, that lets the variance exceed the mean instead of forcing them to be equal
The practical rule: when the data is this overdispersed, reach for negative binomial, not plain Poisson — you don’t need to derive why, just recognise the symptom (variance ≫ mean) and know the fix exists

text:
Fitting it, in code
nb_model = smf.negativebinomial(
    "cnt ~ temp_c + workingday + C(season_name) + windspeed + hum",
    data=df
).fit()
α comes out estimated by maximum likelihood, not assumed — here, .

Other kinds of y, briefly

Ordinal/nominal outcomes (e.g. satisfaction ratings, product categories) can sometimes be recast as binary — “top box vs. not” — trading some information for a model you already know how to run
Duration variables (time until an event) are often censored — you don’t observe the full duration for everyone. Running OLS on censored durations gets the direction right but not the magnitude. Converting to a binary “did the event happen by time T” is often the pragmatic choice

title: GLMs — Count Outcomes
text:
Summary

A count outcome needs a link function that keeps predictions non-negative — the log link, giving Poisson regression
Coefficients are read via the incidence rate ratio, \(\exp(\beta)\) — the same logic as an odds ratio, just multiplicative on counts
Poisson assumes variance equals the mean — check this before trusting the standard errors, since real data is often far more dispersed than that
Negative binomial is the standard fix, and it can move both the standard errors and the estimates themselves

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Causal analysis and experiments
Every regression this module has described association carefully, and stopped short of claiming an effect. This week: a formal framework for when you’re allowed to make that claim.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
section: Does working from home change who quits?
text:
Does working from home change who quits?

Business question: you’re deciding whether to let staff work from home. Would it actually change how many people quit — or is it just a perk that changes nothing?


We have real data: a company that ran this as an actual experiment on 249 of its own employees.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
The naive answer
Naive answer: compare the quit rate of employees who already work from home to those who don’t.

Why it’s not that simple: people who already work from home chose to. They might have longer commutes, different family situations, different tenure — any of which could explain a lower quit rate on its own. This is exactly the naive comparison Week 6 taught us to distrust.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
What we need

A formal definition of what “the effect of X” actually means
A way to know, not just hope, that two groups are comparable
The tools to work with data collected this way — an experiment — properly

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text: The potential outcomes framework

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
What makes a question causal

Causality requires two things: an intervention that’s at least conceptually possible, and variation in it across subjects
“Do vitamins have a beneficial health effect?” — intervention: taking vitamins or not
“Does better management yield greater revenue?” — intervention: replacing or training managers
“Does a major industrial investment affect nearby house prices?” — intervention: the investment itself
If neither an intervention nor variation is conceivable, the question isn’t answerable causally — it might still be worth describing, just not with this toolkit


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 19

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Treatment, subjects, outcome

The causal variable — usually an intervention: a price change, an ad, a policy change. Also called the treatment
The subjects — who or what receives it. Some are treated, some are untreated; both groups matter equally
The outcome — what might be affected
A precise causal question names both: what’s \(Y\)? What’s \(X\)?

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Two states of the world
Every subject has two potential outcomes:
\[y_i^1 \text{ — what happens if treated} \qquad y_i^0 \text{ — what happens if not}\]

Before the intervention happens, both exist — hypothetically, for every subject, whether or not they’ll actually end up treated.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
What assignment reveals

Once a subject is assigned — treated or not — one potential outcome becomes real and observable
The other stops being knowable. It isn’t hidden somewhere in the data; it never gets realised at all
Treated subject: observed outcome = their treated outcome \(y_i^1\)
Untreated subject: observed outcome = their untreated outcome \(y_i^0\)


The unobserved one is the counterfactual — what would have happened in the universe where this subject’s treatment status was flipped. It never exists in any dataset, no matter how good.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
The individual treatment effect
\[te_i = y_i^1 - y_i^0\]

This can never be measured. Not “hard to measure” — impossible, for anyone, ever, from data alone. We only ever see one of the two potential outcomes per subject. This is a missing-data problem with no fix.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
A worked example

Outcome: did the subject convert (1) or not (0)?
\(te_i\) can only take three values: \(+1\) (converted because of treatment), \(-1\) (converted despite not being treated — treatment would have stopped it), or \(0\) (same outcome either way)
For any specific person, we will never know which of the three is true — only ever one of \(y_i^1, y_i^0\) is observed for them

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Heterogeneous treatment effects

Individual effects vary, of course — by subgroup, by circumstance, by person
Men vs. women, small markets vs. large ones, new employees vs. long-tenured ones
The possibility that effects differ across subjects is the normal case, not an edge case worth ignoring


We can’t recover the full distribution of \(te_i\). But we can recover its average.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
The average treatment effect
\[ATE = E[y_i^1] - E[y_i^0]\]

The average, across everyone, of the individual effects — even though we can’t see any individual one
Multiply by population size to get the total effect of rolling something out

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
section: Averages of differences = differences of averages
text:
Averages of differences = differences of averages
\[ATE = E[te_i] = E[y_i^1 - y_i^0] = E[y_i^1] - E[y_i^0]\]

This identity is what rescues the whole framework. We can’t average something we can’t observe (\(te_i\), person by person). But we can separately average the treated group’s outcomes and the untreated group’s outcomes — and their difference equals the same thing.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
ATE can hide heterogeneity

If \(ATE = 0\), did the intervention genuinely do nothing?


Not necessarily. \(ATE = 0\) is consistent with every individual effect being exactly zero — or with the intervention helping half the subjects and hurting the other half by equal amounts. The average alone can’t tell these apart.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Subgroups and ATET

ATE can be calculated for any subgroup, not just the whole population
One especially useful subgroup: the treated group itself
\(ATET\) — average treatment effect on the treated — answers “was this decision worth it, for the people it was actually applied to?” rather than “what would it do to a randomly chosen person?”


Under random assignment, \(ATE = ATET\) — Section C explains why.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
section: When X isn’t just on or off
text:
When X isn’t just on or off

Not every intervention is binary. Examples: prices, advertising budgets, dosages, days per week working from home
These are quantitative causal variables — the intervention doesn’t just happen or not, its size varies too

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
section: A series of individual effects, not one
text:
A series of individual effects, not one

With a quantitative \(x\), there’s no single \(te_i\) — the effect depends on how much \(x\) changes, and where you start from
Before we can even average, we need an extra step: define the effect per unit change in \(x\), for each subject
Everything else — heterogeneity, ATE, the same “average of differences = difference of averages” identity — carries over once that per-unit effect is defined


Our case study today is binary (WFH: yes or no) precisely because it keeps this first pass simple. The same logic extends to “how many days” — just with one extra step.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Ceteris paribus, formalised

“All else equal” has been this module’s working principle since Week 4. Potential outcomes is the same idea, made precise: the difference between \(y_i^1\) and \(y_i^0\) is the intervention and only the intervention — nothing else about the subject is allowed to differ
The question of what needs to stay fixed and what’s allowed to vary is exactly the causal question — there’s no way to answer it from the data alone

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Ceteris paribus vs. multivariate regression
Recall Week 6’s regression:
\[y^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 z\]

In regression, we condition on \(z\): compare two observations with the same \(z\) but different \(x\)
That comparison is exactly what ceteris paribus means — holding \(z\) fixed, letting only \(x\) vary


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 19

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Can regression actually deliver it?

Can we condition on every potential confounder in a regression?


Probably not. We can only include what we actually observed in the data — and ceteris paribus, strictly, means holding everything fixed, measured or not. This is the honest gap between the theoretical ideal and any real regression, no matter how many controls it has.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
What to do?

\(te_i\) can never be calculated or averaged directly, and true ceteris paribus is a theoretical concept we can only approximate — how to get a good estimate of ATE is the central technical problem this module keeps returning to
Everything from here is about closing that gap as much as the data allows

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text: Mapping it with DAGs

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
Causal Analysis and Experiments
section: Why draw the map at all?
text:
Why draw the map at all?

A causal map’s job is to summarise your assumptions about how variables affect each other — assumptions you’re making anyway, every time you choose what goes into a regression
Once the map is drawn, deciding what belongs in the model stops being guesswork
Every “control for X” decision this module has made since Week 6 was implicitly assuming a DAG. This section makes that assumption explicit — and gives you a rule, not a gut feeling


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 19

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments

section: Confounder or mediator — which is it here?
text:
Confounder or mediator — which is it here?

Back to working from home. Suppose it reduces commute stress, and commute stress affects whether someone quits. Is commute stress a confounder of the WFH → quit relationship, or a mediator?


A mediator — it sits downstream of the treatment, part of how WFH works, not a pre-existing difference between the groups. This is exactly why Section D’s regression compared quit rates by assignment alone, with no other controls: random assignment already handles the confounders, and there’s no mediator sitting between assignment and outcome to accidentally control away.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text: Random assignment — the solution

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Why random assignment works

If treatment is assigned independently of potential outcomes — for a reason that has nothing to do with what would have happened either way — then the treated and untreated groups are, on average, identical except for treatment
Under random assignment, the simple difference in observed averages is a good estimate of the ATE
This is a theoretical guarantee, not something you can verify directly in any one dataset — there’s no test that proves assignment was random, only reasons to believe it

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Experimenting versus conditioning

Experimental data: variation in \(x\) is controlled by the experimenter — deliberately made exogenous
Observational data: variation in \(x\) comes from wherever it comes from — some of it exogenous, some of it tangled up with \(y\) itself. The best we can do is condition on what we can measure, exactly as Weeks 4–8 have been doing
A controlled experiment is the most direct way to get exogenous variation in \(x\). Everything else is a second-best attempt at the same goal


This is why the rest of this session focuses on running experiments well — and why the online session comes back to what’s left when you can’t.

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text: Designing and running the experiment

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
The experiment family

Field experiments — as close to the real decision environment as possible. Our case study today: a real firm, its own employees
Lab experiments — controlled but artificial; higher control, lower realism
A/B tests — a specific kind of field experiment, comparing versions of the same product (a page, an ad, an email). Easy to scale, large N


Most firms still don’t experiment, even though the potential is huge — internet firms are the biggest exception, running randomised tests on their own customers constantly.

text:
Case study: working from home

Real firm, real employees. Working from home four days a week — does it change whether staff quit, and how they perform?

Randomly assigned to work from home or stay in the office:

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
section: How many subjects do you need?
text:
How many subjects do you need?

Sample size depends on: significance level, the power you want (chance of detecting a real effect if it exists), and the minimum effect size worth detecting
Smaller effects need bigger samples — precision doesn’t come free
Gabor’s own worked example for this: fine-tuning social media advertising — a CEU business school choosing between two versions of an ad

from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower

effect_size = proportion_effectsize(0.01, 0.02)  # planning assumption: 1% CTR, want to detect a doubling
n_needed = NormalIndPower().solve_power(effect_size=abs(effect_size), alpha=0.05, power=0.8, ratio=1)


html`<p>Planning assumption: a <strong>${planning_ctr}%</strong> click-through rate. To detect a doubling of that rate at 80% power: <strong>${n_needed.toLocaleString()}</strong> visitors per arm.</p>`

text: Complications

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Imperfect compliance

Gabor’s own account of this experiment: fewer than 20% of the treatment group had to be reassigned back to the office, because of changes in their personal circumstances.


Assignment (what a subject is told to do) and treatment (what they actually do) don’t always match
With small non-compliance like this, the effect we measured — comparing by assignment — is a reasonable stand-in for the effect of actual treatment
With substantial non-compliance, that stops being true, and the honest move is to say so rather than report a number that’s no longer trustworthy

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
ITT versus the treatment effect

What we measured above compares people by assignment, regardless of what they actually did — this is the intent-to-treat (ITT) effect
ITT answers a genuinely useful question on its own: “if we rolled this out and got this level of compliance, what would happen?” — often the more decision-relevant number anyway
The LATE (local average treatment effect) — the effect specifically on those who comply with their assignment — is what you’d need instead if non-compliance were large

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Being observed changes behaviour

Hawthorne effect: both treated and untreated subjects change their behaviour simply because they know they’re being watched — not because of the treatment itself
John Henry effect: the control group works harder than usual, specifically because they know they’re the comparison — the opposite problem, and just as real
Spillovers: one subject’s treatment can affect another’s outcome directly — breaks the clean comparison entirely. Good design keeps treatment and control apart where possible


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 20

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Internal and external validity

Internal validity here: assignment was random, and non-compliance was small and concentrated in the treatment group only — Gabor judges internal validity as strong for this study
External validity: this firm changed its actual management practice off the back of this result — real impact. But would the same effect hold at a different firm, a different job type, a different country? That’s a judgement call, not something the data itself can answer

This is what a trustworthy causal claim looks like: a real intervention, real random assignment, and a result that would have been just as credible if it had come out null

title: Causal Analysis and Experiments
text:
Summary

Potential outcomes formalise what “an effect” even means — and confirm the individual effect is permanently unobservable, only the average is reachable
DAGs make the causal question, and the assumptions behind it, explicit
Random assignment is what makes the simple group comparison trustworthy — everything else this module has done with observational data is a second-best attempt at the same goal
Real experiments still need care: enough power, checked balance, and an honest reckoning with imperfect compliance

title: When You Can’t Randomise
text:
When you can’t randomise
The workshop showed the gold standard. Most of the time, you won’t have it — the portfolio project almost certainly won’t. This session: the reasoning tools for observational data, and their honest limits.

title: When You Can’t Randomise
section: Recap: why experiments are the gold standard
text:
Recap: why experiments are the gold standard

Random assignment makes variation in the causal variable exogenous — independent of potential outcomes — which is exactly what makes the simple group comparison trustworthy
Most business questions can’t be experimented on: it’s too slow, too expensive, unethical, or the decision has already been made and you only have the data left over
This is the normal situation, not the exception. The rest of this module’s regression toolkit exists because of it

title: When You Can’t Randomise
text:
The honest fallback

Without random assignment, we can’t create exogenous variation — we can only try to condition it into existence, by controlling for everything endogenous we can measure.
Week 6 called this the difference between omitted variable bias and multicollinearity. This session gives it a proper diagram.

title: When You Can’t Randomise
text: Naming the confounders

title: When You Can’t Randomise
section: Three ways a variable can confound
text:
Three ways a variable can confound

Common-cause confounder: one variable drives both \(x\) and \(y\) — the classic case, and the one Week 6’s OVB formula was built for
Reverse-causality confounder: what looks like \(x \to y\) is partly \(y \to x\) — the direction of the arrow itself is in question
Unwanted-mechanism confounder: \(x\) affects \(y\) through a route that has nothing to do with the causal story you actually care about

Is this causal?

People who eat more fruit and veg aren’t a random sample of the population — they may also earn more, exercise more, smoke less
Gabor’s own version of this question: household income is a plausible common-cause confounder — richer households can afford better diets, and income affects blood pressure through completely different channels (stress, healthcare access, housing)

title: When You Can’t Randomise
text: Latent variables

title: When You Can’t Randomise
text:
The confounder you can’t measure

A latent variable is a confounder that lives in your reasoning but not in your data — “ability,” “motivation,” “management quality”
If it’s correlated with \(x\), leaving it out is still omitted variable bias — the fact that you can’t measure it doesn’t make the bias go away
Sometimes a rough proxy is available (years of education for ability, a past sales figure for motivation) — imperfect, but better than nothing


This is precisely the ceiling Week 6’s worked example (the gender pay gap) hit — multiple regression closes the gap between naive and adjusted estimates, but only for what’s actually in the data.

title: When You Can’t Randomise
text: Bad controls

title: When You Can’t Randomise
text:
Not every correlated variable belongs
Week 6 first raised this with the TV-advertising example. Three specific shapes are worth naming:

Exogenous-source variable: unaffected by \(x\), unrelated to \(y\) except by chance — controlling for it does no harm, but doesn’t help either
Mechanism (mediator) variable: sits on the causal path from \(x\) to \(y\) — controlling for it removes part of the very effect you’re trying to measure
Collider variable: caused by both \(x\) and \(y\) — controlling for it can create a spurious association where none existed

title: When You Can’t Randomise
When You Can’t Randomise
section: Telling them apart is genuinely hard
text:
Telling them apart is genuinely hard

There’s no shortcut that avoids thinking about the DAG. The question to ask of every control variable: does this sit upstream of \(x\) (a legitimate confounder to include), or downstream / on the path (a bad control to exclude)?
If you can’t draw the arrow with confidence, that’s a sign to say so explicitly in your write-up, not to guess.

title: When You Can’t Randomise
text: A middle ground, briefly

title: When You Can’t Randomise
text:
Natural experiments

Occasionally, real-world events create variation that behaves as if it were randomly assigned — a policy change, a lottery, a sharp eligibility cutoff — without the analyst designing anything
These sit between pure observation and a controlled experiment, and support genuinely credible causal claims when the “as-if-random” story holds up
This module doesn’t go further into the specific designs (difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity) — worth knowing the name exists, and worth reading about if your own portfolio project stumbles across a setting where one might apply, but it’s out of scope here

title: When You Can’t Randomise
text:
Summary

Confounders come in three shapes: common cause, reverse causality, unwanted mechanism — and only the first is what Week 6’s OVB formula directly targets
Latent variables are confounders you can’t measure — they don’t stop being confounders for being invisible
Bad controls (mechanism variables, colliders) can make a model worse even though they’re correlated with \(y\) — more controls isn’t automatically better
When you can’t randomise, the honest move is naming what you couldn’t control for, not pretending the model closes every gap

Week 10: Prediction

A different goal again — not explaining the past, but forecasting what comes next

title: Prediction
text:
Prediction
Every model so far has answered “what’s the relationship?” This week asks a different question: “what’s my best guess for this new observation?”

title: Prediction
text:
Selling your car

Business question: You want to sell your Toyota Camry through an online ad. What price do you put in the listing?


You have data on hundreds of other Camrys already advertised — their age, mileage, condition, and asking price. Somewhere in that data is the answer.

title: Prediction
text:
The naive answer
Naive answer: run a regression of price on the car’s features, read off the coefficients, plug in your car’s numbers.

Why it’s not that simple: which features? How many? A model with more variables always fits the data in front of you better — but does it give a better price for your car, or just a better description of the cars you already have data on?

title: Prediction
section: Explanation and prediction are different goals
text:
Explanation and prediction are different goals
Every regression so far has asked: what is the relationship, and can we trust the coefficients?

This week asks something else: given a new car we haven’t seen, what’s our best guess for its price?

We care much less about individual coefficients, or multicollinearity between them
We care much more about whether \(\hat y\) is close to the true \(y\) for new observations
The best model for explaining is not always the best model for predicting



Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 13

title: Prediction
text:
What we need

A way to measure how wrong a prediction is, and how much that should matter
A way to tell whether a model that fits well is actually a good model, or just an overfit one
A rule for choosing between models that doesn’t just reward complexity

title: Prediction
text: Setting up the problem

title: Prediction
text:
Original data and live data

Original data — what we have: cars with known prices, used to build the model
Live data — the observations the model will actually be applied to once it’s built: your car, or the next ad posted tomorrow. We know their \(x\)’s, but not yet their \(y\) — that’s the whole point of predicting them. The model is only useful if the relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) in the live data matches what it learned from the original data.
Target variable \(y\) — what we want to predict (price)
Predictor variables \(x\) — what we use to predict it (age, mileage, condition…)


\[\hat y_j = \hat f(x_j)\]
We need a predicted value for target observation \(j\) — we know its \(x\)’s, we don’t know its \(y\).

title: Prediction
text:
The prediction error
The prediction error is the gap between what the model says and what actually happens — the single number that tells you how wrong a specific prediction was, once you find out:
\[e_j = \hat y_j - y_j\]

Direction of miss: positive if we overpredict, negative if we underpredict — whether that matters depends on the decision
Size of miss: larger in absolute value the further the prediction is from the truth
The prediction error is unknown until the actual value is realised — that’s the whole problem

title: Prediction
text:
Decomposing the prediction error
Three sources, stacked together:

Estimation error — we don’t know the true \(\beta\)’s, only estimates. Shrinks with a larger sample.
Model error — we may not have the best model: wrong functional form, missing an interaction, wrong variables entirely.
Irreducible (genuine) error — the part no model could ever capture, even with the truth known exactly.


Estimation and model error are the two parts an analyst can actually improve.

title: Prediction
text:
Point and interval prediction

A point prediction is a single number — the price to put in the ad
An interval prediction captures the uncertainty around it
The 95% prediction interval covers estimation error and irreducible error — but not model error. It assumes the model itself is right.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 13

title: Prediction
text: The loss function

title: Prediction
text:
Turning errors into a decision
A loss function attaches a value to a prediction error — how bad is being wrong by this much, in this direction?

Two questions decide its shape:

Symmetric? Are errors in opposite directions equally bad?
Convex? Does an error twice as large cost more than twice as much?

title: Prediction
Prediction
section: Would either example change your loss function?
text:
Would either example change your loss function?

Selling your car: a too-low price sells fast but leaves money on the table; a too-high price means waiting, and maybe revising the price down later. What loss function fits that?
A bank deciding on a loan: rejecting a debtor who would have repaid costs a missed opportunity; approving one who defaults costs real money directly. Are those two kinds of error the same size?

title: Prediction
text:
Mean squared error and RMSE
For \(K\) target observations, \(\hat y_k\) is the model’s prediction for observation \(k\) and \(y_k\) its actual value:
\[MSE = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}(\hat y_k - y_k)^2 \qquad RMSE = \sqrt{MSE}\]

Squared loss is symmetric and convex — the most widely used loss function
\(MSE\) minimisation is exactly what OLS already does — that’s why the average is the best predictor under squared loss
\(RMSE\) is easier to interpret: it’s back in the original units (dollars, not dollars²)

title: Prediction
section: MSE decomposes into bias and variance
text:
MSE decomposes into bias and variance
\(\overline{\hat y} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_k \hat y_k\) — the average prediction across all \(K\) target observations, not any one \(\hat y_k\) on its own. That lets us write the bias compactly: \(\bar e = \overline{\hat y} - \bar y\), the average of the individual prediction errors \(e_k = \hat y_k - y_k\).
\[MSE = \underbrace{\bar e^{\,2}}_{\text{Bias}^2} \; + \; \underbrace{\frac{1}{K}\sum_k (e_k - \bar e)^2}_{\text{Prediction variance}}\]

Bias (\(\bar e\)): the average prediction error across all \(K\) observations. Zero for an unbiased predictor.
Variance: how much each error \(e_k\) varies around that average — not how much \(y\) itself varies.
OLS is unbiased. Some other methods (LASSO, later this week’s online session) trade a little bias for a lot less variance.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 13

title: Prediction
text: Overfitting

title: Prediction
text:
Underfit, overfit
Comparing two models on the same data:

Underfitting: Model A fits worse than Model B, in both the original data and the live data. Simple — build a better model.
Overfitting: Model A actually fits better in the original data, but worse in the live data. This is the dangerous one — it looks like the better model until it’s too late to tell.


Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 13

title: Prediction
text:
Why overfitting happens
Typically: a model too complex for the data — too many variables, too many interactions, too flexible a functional form (high-degree polynomials, splines with too many knots).

It fits patterns that are:

specific to this sample, not the general pattern behind it (an internal validity problem), or
specific to the world of the original data, not the world the live data comes from (an external validity problem)

title: Prediction
text:
How would we actually know?
In-sample RMSE can’t catch overfitting — it’s measured on the same data the model was fit to, so it rewards complexity by construction.

We don’t have live data yet, but we can pretend: hold back some of the original data, fit the model without it, then see how well the model predicts the part it never saw.
Do that a few times and average the results — that’s what the chart’s cross-validated RMSE line means. The full mechanics come shortly.

title: Prediction
section: The complexity curve, on our own data

title: Prediction
text: Finding the best model

title: Prediction
text:
Two ways to penalise complexity
Approach 1 — indirectly. Fit on all the data, use a fit measure with a built-in penalty for the number of parameters.
Approach 2 — directly. Actually hold data back, and see how the model does on data it never saw.

title: Prediction
text:
The BIC (and AIC)
Both take the same starting point — the model’s log-likelihood — and add a penalty for the number of parameters, \(k\):
\[AIC = -2 \times \ln(likelihood) + 2 \times k \qquad\qquad BIC = -2 \times \ln(likelihood) + \ln(N) \times k\]

Same idea, different penalty: BIC’s penalty (\(\ln N\) per parameter) is heavier than AIC’s (a flat 2 per parameter) once \(N > 7\)
No sample splitting needed — useful when data is limited
The likelihood requires a distributional assumption — for OLS, that the residuals are normally distributed. Neither AIC nor BIC is free: this is the price for not having to hold data back.
Don’t use plain \(R^2\) or MSE for model choice — they never penalise complexity, so they always favour the most complex model
In practice, this course uses BIC, not AIC — Gabor & Kézdi’s own recommendation

k-fold cross-validation
Rather than one split, do it \(k\) times:

Divide the data into \(k\) roughly equal folds
For each fold: train on the other \(k-1\) folds, test on this one, record the RMSE
Average the \(k\) RMSEs — this is the cross-validated RMSE


Every observation gets used for both training and testing, just never both at once. Less sensitive to which particular split you happened to draw.

title: Model Building for Prediction

Log or level?

When price is the target, its relationship with predictors is often closer to linear once expressed as \(\ln(price)\)
Log differences approximate relative (percentage) differences — often more stable across a wide price range
Technical bonus: log prices are often closer to normally distributed, which helps a linear regression approximate the average well

title: Model Building for Prediction
section: The correction that’s easy to forget
text:
The correction that’s easy to forget
If the target was modelled in logs, the model predicts \(\widehat{\ln y}\) — not \(\hat y\). Simply exponentiating underestimates the average:
\[\hat y_j = e^{\widehat{\ln y}_j} \times e^{\hat\sigma^2/2}\]

\(e^{\widehat{\ln y}}\) alone recovers the median, not the mean
The correction term adjusts for the spread of the regression’s residuals — bigger residual variance, bigger correction
Skipping it silently biases every prediction downward

text: LASSO

title: Model Building for Prediction
text:
We can’t try every model

With \(p\) candidate predictors, the number of possible models explodes — this is an NP-hard problem, not just a big one
By hand: domain knowledge drives the choice — interpretable, but slow, and impossible with many interactions
By algorithm: let the data suggest which variables earn their place

title: Model Building for Prediction
text:
The LASSO idea
LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) adds a penalty to the usual OLS minimisation:
\[\min_\beta \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{k}\beta_j x_{ij}\right)^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{k}|\beta_j| \right\}\]

The penalty shrinks coefficients toward zero
Coefficients whose inclusion barely improves fit get shrunk all the way to zero — dropped from the model entirely
\(\lambda\) controls how aggressive that is; larger \(\lambda\), fewer surviving variables

title: Model Building for Prediction
text:
The cost: bias

OLS is unbiased. LASSO isn’t — that’s the trade it makes for lower variance
Unlike OLS, there’s no closed-form solution; an algorithm solves for \(\beta\) and \(\lambda\) together
\(\lambda\) itself is chosen by cross-validation: try many values, pick the one with the best CV RMSE


Ridge regression is the same idea with a squared penalty (\(\lambda\sum\beta_j^2\)) instead — it shrinks coefficients but never sets them exactly to zero. LASSO is “L1,” Ridge is “L2.”

Every dataset so far has been a snapshot — many units, one point in time. What changes when it’s one unit, followed through time?

title: Time Series Regression
text:
How risky is Microsoft stock?

Business question: you’re considering investing in Microsoft stock. How much does it move when the overall market moves — and how would you even estimate that?


We have real daily data on Microsoft’s share price and the S&P 500 index, from December 1997 to December 2018.

title: Time Series Regression
text:
The naive answer
Naive answer: regress the Microsoft share price directly on the S&P 500 index level. Read off the slope.

Why it’s not that simple: both series have climbed for two decades. Two things that both trend upward will look related whether or not they actually are — and that’s before we’ve even asked whether “same day” is even the right comparison.

title: Time Series Regression
text:
What we need

An understanding of what makes time series data different from the cross-sections we’ve used all module
A way to tell a genuine relationship apart from two variables that just happen to drift the same direction
The tools to fix it when regression assumptions specific to time series data break down

title: Time Series Regression
section: What’s special about time series data
text: What’s special about time series data

title: Time Series Regression
text:
New notation, new opportunities

Time series data follows one unit across many time periods: \(y_t,\ t = 1, 2, \dots, T\)
Ordering matters — this is the key difference from every cross-section this module has used
New opportunities: we can ask how \(y\) responds to a change in \(x\), immediately or with a delay
New complications: frequency, gaps, and — the big one — values that aren’t independent of their own past

title: Time Series Regression
text:
Trend
\[\Delta y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}\]

Positive trend: \(E[\Delta y_t] > 0\) on average. Negative trend is the mirror image.
Linear trend: the change itself is stable on average
Exponential trend: the relative change is stable on average — common for prices, income, anything that compounds

title: Time Series Regression
text:
Seasonality

The expected value changes periodically — by day of week, month, or hour
Can be linear (constant seasonal gaps) or exponential (constant relative gaps)
Both trend and seasonality make time series regression genuinely harder than cross-sectional regression

title: Time Series Regression
text:
Stationarity
A stationary time series has the same expected value and distribution at every point in time. Stability, full stop.

Non-stationary series break this in one of three ways:

Has a trend
Has seasonality
Has an unstable, ever-widening spread — a random walk

title: Time Series Regression
text:
Random walk
\[y_t = y_{t-1} + e_t\]

Today’s value is yesterday’s value, plus a completely random, unpredictable shock
Whatever happened last period doesn’t influence the size of today’s shock — but \(y_t\) still carries forward everything that came before
The spread of possible values grows the further out you go — genuinely impossible to predict beyond a drift

text: Spurious regression, and fixing it

title: Time Series Regression
section: When correlation is just two trends
text:
When correlation is just two trends

Per-capita cheese consumption correlates at 0.947 with the number of people who died getting tangled in their bedsheets (Tyler Vigen, Spurious Correlations). Neither causes the other — both simply drifted upward over the same years.


Trend and seasonality act like confounders — omitted variables that create an association where none exists. The regression can’t tell the difference between “these move together because they’re related” and “these move together because it’s 2015 for both of them.”

title: Time Series Regression
text:
The fix: differencing

Replace variables in the regression with their first differences — this removes the trend and is often enough to make a series stationary
Same idea in relative terms: percent changes, or their close approximation, log differences

\[\Delta y_t^E = \alpha + \beta \Delta x_t\]

\(\alpha\): how much \(y\) changes on average when \(x\) doesn’t change. \(\beta\): how much more \(y\) changes when \(x\) changes by one more unit — additional to \(\alpha\), not instead of it.

title: Time Series Regression
text:
The fix: seasonal dummies

Differencing handles trend. Seasonality needs its own fix — include a dummy for each season (month, day of week, whatever the cycle is)

\[y_t^E = \alpha + \beta x_t + \delta_{Jan} + \delta_{Feb} + \dots + \delta_{Nov}\]

One category held out as reference, exactly like any other categorical variable since Week 6

text: Serial correlation

title: Time Series Regression
text:
Correlated with its own past
\[\rho_1 = Corr[y_t, y_{t-1}]\]

Serial correlation: a variable correlated with its own lagged values
\(\rho_1 = 0\) means no serial correlation — “white noise,” order doesn’t matter, just like cross-sectional data
Positive serial correlation: if \(y_t\) is above average, \(y_{t+1}\) is more likely to be above average too

title: Time Series Regression
section: Why this breaks the standard errors
text:
Why this breaks the standard errors

Serial correlation doesn’t bias the coefficient — but it makes the usual standard errors wrong, often badly so
Even heteroskedasticity-robust SEs (the HC1 we’ve used since Week 5) don’t fix this — a different problem needs a different tool


Two fixes:

Newey-West standard errors — built to handle serial correlation directly (and heteroskedasticity too), needs a choice of how many lags to account for. In statsmodels, this is cov_type="HAC" (Heteroskedasticity- and Autocorrelation-Consistent) with cov_kwds={"maxlags": ...} — “HAC” is the library’s name for the Newey-West family, not a different thing.
Include a lagged dependent variable in the regression itself — usually one lag is enough

title: Time Series Regression
section: When effects take time to arrive
text:
When effects take time to arrive

A lagged association: \(x\) affects \(y\) not immediately, but one or more periods later
Useful whenever there’s a real-world delay — people don’t necessarily change behaviour the moment conditions change

\[\Delta y_t^E = \alpha + \beta_0 \Delta x_t + \beta_1 \Delta x_{t-1} + \beta_2 \Delta x_{t-2}\]
\(\beta_0\): same-period effect. \(\beta_1\): how much more \(y\) changes next period after \(x\) moved, holding \(x\) fixed elsewhere. The cumulative effect is \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 + \beta_2\).

Summary

Time series data brings genuine opportunities — same-unit comparisons over time — and genuine hazards: trend, seasonality, and random walk all threaten spurious results

Serial correlation doesn’t bias coefficients, but breaks standard errors — Newey-West SEs or a lagged DV both fix it
Effects can arrive with a delay — lags let a regression capture that directly

Planning next year’s staffing

Business question: a swimming pool operator needs to know roughly how many tickets will sell each day next year, to plan staffing and opening hours.


Forecasting is a special case of prediction — using only what’s happened up to today to say something about tomorrow. Same discipline as Week 10’s prediction content, applied to data where “the future” has a very literal meaning.

text: Forecast horizon and cross-validation

title: Forecasting from Time Series Data
text:
Forecast horizon

The length of the live time series data still to come — the forecast horizon, \(H\)
Short-horizon: a few periods ahead relative to the data (5 years of monthly data, forecast 3–12 months)
Long-horizon: many periods ahead (5 years of daily data, forecast a year out)

title: Forecasting from Time Series Data
section: Why you can’t just shuffle and split
text:
Why you can’t just shuffle and split
Cross-validation with time series is necessary — and genuinely tricky, because a random shuffle destroys the one thing that makes it a time series: order.

Two approaches, matched to the horizon:

Insert test sets — for long-horizon forecasts, where serial correlation and trend matter less. Use all remaining observations, including those after the test set, as training data.
Rolling window — for short-horizon forecasts, where serial correlation matters. Training data always precedes the test set, so nothing “sees the future.”

section: Two ways to model a trend
text:
Two ways to model a trend

Average change: \(\hat y_{T+H} = y_T + H \times \widehat{\Delta y}\) — carries forward from the last observation
Trend line: \(\hat y_t = \hat\alpha + \hat\delta t\) — assumes \(y\) stays close to a fitted line, so one unusual last observation matters less
Neither is inherently better — depends whether you trust the series to keep going from where it is, or to revert to its long-run pattern

title: Forecasting from Time Series Data
text:
Autoregressive models
\[y_t^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 y_{t-1}\]

The simplest AR(1) model: today’s value predicted from yesterday’s alone
\(\beta_1\) is just the first-order serial correlation coefficient from the workshop, wearing a forecasting hat
\(\beta_1 = 1\) is a random walk; \(\beta_1 = 0\) is white noise — nothing left to forecast from the series itself

title: Forecasting from Time Series Data
text:
The innovation
\[e_t = y_t - y_t^E \qquad y_t = y_t^E + e_t\]
The innovation: what’s genuinely new in \(y_t\), on top of everything predictable from its own past. Formally the same idea as a prediction error — but now it’s past innovations doing the predicting.

title: Forecasting from Time Series Data
text:
ARIMA, built from three letters

AR(p): predict \(y_t\) from up to \(p\) of its own lags
I(d): whether the model is written in \(y\) itself (\(d=0\)) or its \(d\)-th difference
MA(q): a linear combination of past innovations, \(y_t = e_t + \theta_1 e_{t-1} + \dots + \theta_q e_{t-q}\) — captures serial correlation that drops to zero sharply after a few lags, a different pattern than AR
ARIMA(p,d,q) combines all three, flexible enough to approximate almost any serial correlation pattern

text: VAR — bringing in other variables

title: Forecasting from Time Series Data
text:
Forecasting with help from x

Short-horizon forecasts often improve with other variables — but now you need forecasts of those too
Vector autoregression (VAR): a set of time series regressions, one per variable, where every equation’s right-hand side is lags of every variable in the system

\[y_t^E = \beta_{10} + \beta_{11}y_{t-1} + \beta_{12}x_{t-1} \qquad x_t^E = \beta_{20} + \beta_{21}y_{t-1} + \beta_{22}x_{t-1}\]

More coefficients to estimate means more estimation error — the hope is that \(x\) still nets out an improvement

title: Forecasting from Time Series Data
section: The one assumption everything rests on
text:
The one assumption everything rests on

External validity in forecasting means stationarity: the patterns you learned from the training data — trend, seasonality, correlation structure — have to still hold in the live data
This is a much bigger risk in time series than in cross-sectional prediction, because forecasting is by design about a period you’ve never observed
No amount of cross-validation on historical data can fully rule this out — a genuine structural break (a pandemic, a housing crash) breaks every model here equally

title: Forecasting from Time Series Data
text:
Summary

Forecasting is prediction with a time index — but cross-validation has to respect order: inserted test sets for long horizons, rolling windows for short ones
Long-horizon forecasts lean on trend and seasonality — often seasonality alone does most of the work
Short-horizon forecasts lean on serial correlation — AR and ARIMA models capture it directly, chosen by holdout RMSE like any other prediction model
VAR can improve a forecast by bringing in other variables, at the cost of needing to forecast those too — and whether it actually helps is itself an empirical, not automatic, question

title: Inference: When is a Difference Real?
section: What if we had 15,000 students, not ?
text:
What if we had 15,000 students, not ?

With a huge sample, almost any difference becomes statistically significant — the CI narrows to nearly nothing, and even a 1ms gap could reject \(H_0\).


Statistical significance ≠ practical significance. At scale, the question shifts from “is there a difference?” to “is the difference big enough to matter?” — external validity remains just as important as it was at n=.
